docs.title: 45. Explain Promise.all() vs Promise.allSettled().
docs.text:
• Promise.all(iterable): Waits for all to resolve. Rejects immediately if any promise rejects (fail-fast).
  • Promise.allSettled(iterable): Waits for all to finish (resolve or reject). Returns an array of status objects.

docs.title: 46. What is Promise.race()?
docs.text: Returns a promise that resolves or rejects as soon as one of the promises in the iterable resolves or rejects.

docs.title: 47. Explain async and await.
docs.text:
Syntactic sugar built on top of Promises to write asynchronous code that looks synchronous. * async function returns a Promise. * await pauses execution until the Promise resolves.

async function fetchData() {
    try {
        const response = await fetch('/api');
        const data = await response.json();
    } catch (error) {
        console.error(error);
    }
}

docs.title: 48. What happens if you await a non-promise?
docs.text: It is converted to a resolved Promise automatically. const x = await 5; // x is 5

docs.title: 49. Can you use await inside a loop?
docs.text: Yes. * forEach: async callbacks run in parallel (doesn't wait). * for...of: await inside pauses the loop (sequential execution).

docs.title: 50. What is a Microtask vs Macrotask?
docs.text:
• Microtasks: Promises, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver. (High priority, run immediately after current script).
  • Macrotasks: setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate, I/O. (Run in next Event Loop tick).

Execution Order: Script -> All Microtasks -> Render -> One Macrotask.

docs.title: 51. What is the output?
docs.text:
console.log(1);
setTimeout(() => console.log(2), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(3));
console.log(4);
Answer: 1, 4, 3, 2 (Sync -> Sync -> Microtask -> Macrotask).

docs.title: 52. What is setTimeout?
docs.text: Schedules code to be run after a specified delay (in ms). It is not part of JS engine, but a Web API provided by the browser/Node environment.

docs.title: 53. Why is setTimeout(fn, 0) useful?
docs.text: It pushes the function to the end of the Call Stack (to the task queue), allowing the UI to update or the current execution to finish first.

docs.title: 54. What is Callback Hell?
docs.text: The situation where callbacks are nested within other callbacks several levels deep, making code difficult to read and maintain. Solution: Use Promises or Async/Await.

docs.title: 55. What is fetch API?
docs.text: A modern interface for making HTTP requests (replacement for XMLHttpRequest). It returns a Promise.

docs.title: 56. How do you cancel a fetch request?
docs.text:
Using an AbortController.

const controller = new AbortController();
fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal });
controller.abort(); // Cancels request

docs.title: 57. What is JSON.parse and JSON.stringify?
docs.text:
• JSON.parse(): Parses a JSON string to a JS object.
  • JSON.stringify(): Converts a JS object to a JSON string.

docs.title: 58. What is debouncing?
docs.text:
Ensures that a function is not called again until a certain amount of time has passed since it was last called. (e.g., search input).

function debounce(func, delay) {
    let timeout;
    return (...args) => {
        clearTimeout(timeout);
        timeout = setTimeout(() => func(...args), delay);
    };
}

docs.title: 59. What is throttling?
docs.text: Ensures that a function is called at most once in a specified time period. (e.g., window resize, scroll).

docs.title: 60. What is a Generator Function in async context?
docs.text: Generators (function*) can yield Promises. Before async/await, libraries like co used generators to mimic sync-style async code.

docs.title: 61. What is the DOM?
docs.text: Document Object Model. A tree structure representation of the HTML document. It allows JS to manipulate content, structure, and style.

docs.title: 62. How to select elements in DOM?
docs.text:
• document.getElementById('id')
  • document.getElementsByClassName('class')
  • document.getElementsByTagName('div')
  • document.querySelector('.class') (Returns first match)
  • document.querySelectorAll('.class') (Returns NodeList)

docs.title: 63. NodeList vs HTMLCollection?
docs.text:
• HTMLCollection: Live (updates automatically if DOM changes). Returned by getElementsByClassName.
  • NodeList: Static (mostly). Returned by querySelectorAll.

docs.title: 64. What is Event Bubbling?
docs.text: When an event triggers on an element, it first runs the handlers on it, then on its parent, then all the way up on other ancestors. (Bottom -> Up).

docs.title: 65. What is Event Capturing (Trickling)?
docs.text: The opposite of bubbling. The event goes down to the element. (Top -> Down). Enabled by passing { capture: true } to addEventListener.

docs.title: 66. How to stop propagation?
docs.text: event.stopPropagation() stops the event from moving to the next part of the propagation flow (bubbling or capturing).

docs.title: 67. What is event.preventDefault()?
docs.text: Prevents the browser's default behavior for the event (e.g., prevents form submission, or link navigation).

docs.title: 68. What is Event Delegation?
docs.text:
Instead of attaching event listeners to individual elements, you attach a single listener to a common parent. It utilizes event bubbling to handle events for child elements (even dynamically added ones).

document.getElementById('list').addEventListener('click', (e) => {
    if (e.target.tagName === 'LI') {
        console.log('List item clicked');
    }
});

docs.title: 69. What is the dataset property?
docs.text:
Allows access to custom data attributes (data-*) on elements.

<div id="user" data-id="123" data-role="admin"></div>
<script>
    const el = document.getElementById('user');
    console.log(el.dataset.id); // "123"
</script>

docs.title: 70. innerHTML vs innerText vs textContent?
docs.text:
• innerHTML: Parses HTML string (Security risk: XSS).
  • innerText: Visible text (aware of CSS styling like display: none).
  • textContent: All text (including hidden elements). Faster.

docs.title: 71. What is the BOM (Browser Object Model)?
docs.text: Objects provided by the browser to interact with everything outside the page content. Examples: window, navigator, location, history, screen.

docs.title: 72. How do you detect the browser name?
docs.text: navigator.userAgent. (Though feature detection is preferred over browser detection).

docs.title: 73. What is localStorage vs sessionStorage?
docs.text:
• localStorage: Data persists even after the browser is closed. (No expiration).
  • sessionStorage: Data survives page refresh but is cleared when the tab/window is closed.

docs.title: 74. What are Cookies?
docs.text: Small data stored in the browser. Sent with every HTTP request to the server. Properties: Expires, HttpOnly (secure against XSS), Secure (HTTPS only).

docs.title: 75. How to create a new DOM element?
docs.text: document.createElement('tagName').

docs.title: 76. What is a DocumentFragment?
docs.text: A lightweight, minimal document object. It has no parent. Appending to it doesn't cause reflow. Appending the fragment to DOM moves all its children. Used for performance optimization when adding multiple elements.

docs.title: 77. What is Reflow and Repaint?
docs.text:
• Reflow (Layout): Calculating positions and geometries of elements. (Expensive).
  • Repaint: Changing visibility (color, background) without changing layout.

docs.title: 78. What is Shadow DOM?
docs.text: Encapsulation mechanism. Allows a hidden DOM tree to be attached to an element. Styles inside Shadow DOM don't leak out, and global styles don't leak in. Basis of Web Components.

docs.title: 79. What is window.onload vs DOMContentLoaded?
docs.text:
• DOMContentLoaded: HTML is parsed and DOM is built. (External scripts/styles might not be loaded).
  • window.onload: Everything is loaded (images, styles, scripts).

docs.title: 80. How does defer and async work in script tags?
docs.text:
• <script>: Blocks parsing, fetches, executes.
  • <script async>: Fetches in parallel, executes as soon as fetched (pauses parsing). Order not guaranteed.
  • <script defer>: Fetches in parallel, executes after HTML parsing is complete. Order guaranteed.

docs.title: 81. What is a Class in ES6?
docs.text:
Syntactic sugar over prototype-based inheritance.

class Person {
    constructor(name) { this.name = name; }
    greet() { return `Hi, ${this.name}`; }
}

docs.title: 82. What are Modules (ESM)?
docs.text: Official standard for modules. * export (Named or Default). * import. * File-based scope. Always strict mode.

docs.title: 83. What are Template Literals?
docs.text: String literals allowing embedded expressions. Enclosed by backticks (`). Supports multi-line strings.

docs.title: 84. What is the Optional Chaining Operator (?.)?
docs.text:
Safely access nested properties. Returns undefined if reference is nullish.

const zip = user?.address?.zipCode;

docs.title: 85. What is the Nullish Coalescing Operator (??)?
docs.text:
Returns the right-hand operand when the left is null or undefined (not just falsy).

const x = 0 ?? 5; // 0
const y = 0 || 5; // 5

docs.title: 86. What is a Symbol?
docs.text: A unique and immutable primitive. Often used as object keys to create private-like properties or avoid name collisions.

docs.title: 87. What is a Proxy?
docs.text:
An object that wraps another object and intercepts operations (like read, write, function call).

const handler = {
    get: (obj, prop) => prop in obj ? obj[prop] : "Not Found"
};
const p = new Proxy({}, handler);

docs.title: 88. What is Reflect?
docs.text: A built-in object that provides methods for interceptable JavaScript operations. Complements Proxy.

docs.title: 89. What is Memory Leak in JS?
docs.text: When objects are no longer needed but are still referenced, preventing Garbage Collection. Causes: Global variables, forgotton timers, closures, detached DOM nodes.

docs.title: 90. How does Garbage Collection work?
docs.text: Mark-and-Sweep: 1. Roots (Global, Stack) are marked. 2. References are traversed and marked. 3. Unmarked objects (unreachable) are swept (deleted).

docs.title: 91. What is BigInt?
docs.text: A primitive for integers larger than 2^53 - 1. Created by appending n. const huge = 1234567890123456789012345678901234567890n;

docs.title: 92. What is globalThis?
docs.text: A standard way to access the global object across environments (window, self, global).

docs.title: 93. What is Currying vs Partial Application?
docs.text:
• Currying: f(a, b, c) -> f(a)(b)(c).
  • Partial App: f(a, b, c) -> g(b, c) (where a is fixed).

docs.title: 94. What is Memoization?
docs.text: Optimization technique. Caching the result of an expensive function call based on arguments and returning the cached result when the same inputs occur again.

docs.title: 95. What is the difference between for...in and for...of?
docs.text:
• for...in: Iterates over keys (enumerable properties). (Works on Objects).
  • for...of: Iterates over values. (Works on Iterables: Array, Map, Set, String).

docs.title: 96. What is TCO (Tail Call Optimization)?
docs.text: An optimization where a recursive function call is the last action in the function. The engine reuses the stack frame. (Supported in Safari, theoretically in ES6 spec).

docs.title: 97. What is a Polyfill?
docs.text: Code that implements a feature on web browsers that do not support the feature.

docs.title: 98. What is Transpilation (Babel)?
docs.text: Converting modern JS (ES6+) code into older JS (ES5) to ensure compatibility with older browsers.

docs.title: 99. What are Worker Threads (Web Workers)?
docs.text: Allow running scripts in background threads, separate from the main execution thread. Prevents UI blocking during heavy computations. They don't have access to DOM.

docs.title: 100. What is Server-Side Rendering (SSR) vs Client-Side Rendering (CSR)?
docs.text:
• CSR: Browser downloads minimal HTML and a JS bundle. JS fetches data and builds the UI. (Slower initial load, faster interaction).
  • SSR: Server renders HTML with data and sends it. (Faster initial load, SEO friendly).

End of Interview Questions

docs.title: Study Guide
docs.text:
To deepen your understanding of these concepts, check out the following resources:

  • Official Documentation: Javascript Docs
  • Internal Style Guide: Javascript Style Guide

docs.title: Kotlin Interview Questions & Answers (100+)
docs.text:
What's on this page

  • Core content for this topic in the Inkorporated enterprise OS.
  • Practical guidance, roles, or standards as applicable.

What this enables

  • Consistent enterprise operations and decision-making.
  • Shared language for humans and cyborg AI agents.

This guide contains 100+ Kotlin interview questions, ranging from basic syntax to advanced concurrency and coroutines. Each question includes a model answer, code examples, and potential follow-up paths based on the candidate's response.

docs.title: 1. What is the difference between val and var?
docs.text:
• val: Immutable reference. Once assigned, it cannot be reassigned. (Similar to final in Java).
  • var: Mutable reference. Can be reassigned.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate mentions 'Immutable'.

    • Follow-up: "Does val mean the object itself is immutable?"
    • Answer: No, val only guarantees the reference is immutable. If the object is a MutableList, you can still add items to it.

  • Path B: Candidate compares to Java.

    • Follow-up: "When would you prefer val over var?"
    • Answer: Always prefer val for thread safety and predictability, unless mutation is strictly required.

docs.title: 2. How does Kotlin handle Null Safety?
docs.text:
Kotlin's type system distinguishes between references that can hold null (nullable references) and those that cannot (non-null references).

Syntax Name Description String Non-nullable Cannot hold null. Compiler error if assigned null. String? Nullable Can hold null.

Key Operators: * ?. (Safe Call) * !! (Not-null Assertion) * ?: (Elvis Operator)

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate mentions !!.
    • Follow-up: "When is it acceptable to use !!?"
    • Answer: Rarely. Only when you are 100% sure the value is not null and the compiler can't deduce it, or in quick prototypes/tests. It throws a NullPointerException if null.

docs.title: 3. What is the Elvis Operator ?:?
docs.text:
It returns the expression on its left if it is not null, otherwise it returns the expression on its right.

val length = text?.length ?: -1

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Control flow.
    • Follow-up: "Can you use return or throw on the right side of ?:?"
    • Answer: Yes, because return and throw are expressions in Kotlin. 
      val name = user.name ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("Name required")

docs.title: 4. What is Type Inference?
docs.text:
The compiler can automatically identify the data type of a variable from the context or the assigned value.

val name = "Kotlin" // Compiler knows this is String

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Limitations.
    • Follow-up: "When must you explicitly specify the type?"
    • Answer: When declaring a variable without initializing it immediately, or when the inferred type is not the desired one (e.g., Long vs Int).

docs.title: 5. What is the difference between const val and val?
docs.text:
• val: Read-only variable, determined at runtime.
  • const val: Compile-time constant. Must be a top-level property or a member of an object (or companion object). Only primitives and String.

docs.title: 6. What are String Templates?
docs.text:
Strings that contain expressions beginning with $.

val i = 10
println("i = $i")
println("i + 1 = ${i + 1}")

docs.title: 7. Explain lateinit vs lazy.
docs.text:
Feature lateinit lazy Mutability var (Mutable) val (Read-only) Type Non-primitive types only Any type Initialization Later in code On first access Thread Safety Not thread-safe by default Thread-safe (synchronized) by default

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Use cases.
    • Follow-up: "Why use lateinit in Android?"
    • Answer: For dependency injection or View initialization in onCreate where you can't initialize at declaration but know it won't be null when used.

docs.title: 8. What are Data Classes?
docs.text:
Classes whose main purpose is to hold data. The compiler automatically derives the following members: * equals() / hashCode() * toString() * componentN() functions (for destructuring) * copy()

data class User(val name: String, val age: Int)

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Inheritance.
    • Follow-up: "Can a Data Class be open or abstract?"
    • Answer: No, data classes are final by default and cannot be open or abstract.

docs.title: 9. What is the difference between == and ===?
docs.text:
• ==: Structural equality. Checks if contents are equal (calls equals()).
  • ===: Referential equality. Checks if variables point to the same object in memory.

docs.title: 10. How does the when expression work?
docs.text:
It replaces the switch operator of C-like languages but is more powerful. It can be used as a statement or an expression.

val result = when (x) {
    1 -> "One"
    in 2..10 -> "Between 2 and 10"
    is String -> "It's a string"
    else -> "Unknown"
}

docs.title: 11. How do loops work in Kotlin?
docs.text:
• For: Iterates over anything that provides an iterator. 
    for (item in collection) print(item)
  • While / Do-While: Standard conditional loops.

docs.title: 12. What are Range Expressions?
docs.text:
Tools to define a range of values.

val r1 = 1..10        // 1 to 10 inclusive
val r2 = 1 until 10   // 1 to 9
val r3 = 10 downTo 1  // 10 to 1
val r4 = 1..10 step 2 // 1, 3, 5, 7, 9

docs.title: 13. How do you define a function?
docs.text:
fun sum(a: Int, b: Int): Int {
    return a + b
}
// Single-expression syntax
fun sum(a: Int, b: Int) = a + b

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Default Arguments.
    • Follow-up: "How do default arguments help compared to Java?"
    • Answer: They reduce the need for method overloading.

docs.title: 14. What are Extension Functions?
docs.text:
They allow you to add new functionality to a class without inheriting from it or using design patterns like Decorator.

fun String.removeFirstLastChar(): String =  this.substring(1, this.length - 1)

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Under the hood.
    • Follow-up: "Does it actually modify the class?"
    • Answer: No, it resolves statically. It's syntactic sugar for a static method that takes the instance as the first parameter.

docs.title: 15. What are Infix Functions?
docs.text:
Functions marked with infix keyword can be called using infix notation (omitting the dot and the parentheses). * Must be member functions or extension functions. * Must have a single parameter.

infix fun Int.plus(x: Int): Int = this + x
// Usage
1 plus 2

docs.title: 16. Explain Classes and Objects in Kotlin.
docs.text: Classes are declared using class. Objects can be: * Object Declaration: Singleton. * Object Expression: Anonymous class.

docs.title: 17. What are the Visibility Modifiers?
docs.text:
• public (Default): Visible everywhere.
  • private: Visible inside file (top-level) or class.
  • protected: Visible in class and subclasses.
  • internal: Visible within the same module.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Internal.
    • Follow-up: "What constitutes a 'module'?"
    • Answer: A Maven/Gradle module, or an IntelliJ IDEA module.

docs.title: 18. Primary vs Secondary Constructors.
docs.text:
• Primary: Part of the class header.
  • Secondary: Prefixed with constructor. Must delegate to the primary constructor (directly or indirectly) using this().

docs.title: 19. How does Inheritance work?
docs.text:
All classes inherit from Any. Classes are final by default. To allow inheritance, mark the class with open.

open class Base(p: Int)
class Derived(p: Int) : Base(p)

docs.title: 20. How are Interfaces different in Kotlin compared to Java 7?
docs.text:
Kotlin interfaces can contain properties and functions with default implementations. They cannot store state.

interface MyInterface {
    val prop: Int // abstract
    fun foo() { print("Default impl") }
}

docs.title: 21. What is the difference between an Abstract Class and an Interface?
docs.text: Feature Abstract Class Interface State Can hold state (fields). Cannot hold state (only properties without backing fields). Constructor Can have constructors. Cannot have constructors. Inheritance Single inheritance. Multiple implementation. Use Case Is-A relationship, sharing state. Can-Do relationship, behavior contract.

docs.title: 22. What are Sealed Classes?
docs.text:
sealed classes represent restricted class hierarchies. All direct subclasses must be known at compile time and declared in the same package (and same module).

Use Case: Perfect for when expressions, ensuring all cases are covered without an else branch.

sealed class Result
data class Success(val data: String) : Result()
data class Error(val exception: Exception) : Result()
object Loading : Result()

docs.title: 23. What is an Object Declaration?
docs.text:
It is Kotlin's way of defining a Singleton.

object DatabaseConfig {
    val url = "jdbc:..."
}
The initialization is thread-safe and lazy (on first access).

docs.title: 24. What is a Companion Object?
docs.text:
An object declared inside a class using the companion keyword. * It is tied to the class, not instances. * Similar to static members in Java. * Can implement interfaces.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Access.
    • Follow-up: "How do you access members of a companion object?"
    • Answer: Simply by using the class name: MyClass.create().

docs.title: 25. What are the requirements for a Data Class?
docs.text:
1. Primary constructor must have at least one parameter.
  2. All primary constructor parameters must be marked as val or var.
  3. Cannot be abstract, open, sealed, or inner.

docs.title: 26. Explain Class Delegation (by keyword).
docs.text:
Kotlin supports the "composition over inheritance" pattern natively. A class can implement an interface by delegating all of its public members to a specified object.

interface Base { fun print() }
class BaseImpl(val x: Int) : Base {
    override fun print() = print(x)
}
class Derived(b: Base) : Base by b

docs.title: 27. What are Higher-Order Functions?
docs.text:
A function that takes another function as a parameter and/or returns a function.

fun calculate(x: Int, y: Int, operation: (Int, Int) -> Int): Int {
    return operation(x, y)
}

docs.title: 28. What is a Lambda Expression?
docs.text:
An anonymous function that can be treated as a value. Syntax: { variable(s) -> body }

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: 'it' keyword.
    • Follow-up: "When can you use it?"
    • Answer: When a lambda has exactly one parameter, you can omit the parameter declaration and refer to it as it.

docs.title: 29. What are Inline Functions?
docs.text:
Using higher-order functions imposes runtime penalties (object allocation for lambdas). The inline modifier tells the compiler to copy the function's code (and the lambda) directly into the call site.

Pros: Performance boost for loop-heavy high-order functions. Cons: Code size increases.

docs.title: 30. What is noinline and crossinline?
docs.text:
• noinline: Used in an inline function to prevent a specific lambda parameter from being inlined.
  • crossinline: Used when a lambda is passed to an inline function but executed in a different context (e.g., inside a nested object or local function), disallowing non-local returns.

docs.title: 31. What are Reified Type Parameters?
docs.text:
In Java, generics are erased at runtime (Type Erasure). In Kotlin, you can use inline functions with reified type parameters to access the type at runtime.

inline fun <reified T> isType(value: Any) = value is T

docs.title: 32. Explain Scope Functions (let, run, with, apply, also).
docs.text:
They execute a block of code within the context of an object.

Function Object Reference Return Value Use Case let it Lambda result Null checks, temporary scope. run this Lambda result Object configuration + computation. with this Lambda result Grouping calls on an object. apply this Object itself Object configuration (builder). also it Object itself Side effects (logging, validation). 
graph TD
    A[Start] --> B{Returns Object?}
    B -- Yes --> C{Ref is 'this'?}
    B -- No --> D{Ref is 'this'?}
    C -- Yes --> E[apply]
    C -- No --> F[also]
    D -- Yes --> G[run / with]
    D -- No --> H[let]

docs.title: 33. What are Destructuring Declarations?
docs.text:
A way to unpack a single composite value into multiple variables.

val (name, age) = user // user must be data class or have componentN functions

docs.title: 34. What is Operator Overloading?
docs.text:
Kotlin allows providing custom implementations for a predefined set of operators (+, -, *, ++, etc.) on user-defined types. You must use the operator modifier.

data class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int) {
    operator fun plus(p: Point) = Point(x + p.x, y + p.y)
}

docs.title: 35. What are Type Aliases?
docs.text:
Provide alternative names for existing types. Useful for shortening long generic types.

typealias NodeSet = Set<Network.Node>
typealias MyHandler = (Int, String, Any) -> Unit

docs.title: 36. Nested vs Inner Classes.
docs.text:
• Nested Class: By default, a class inside another class does not have access to the members of the outer class. (Static nested in Java).
  • Inner Class: Marked with inner. Has reference to the outer class object. Can access members.

docs.title: 37. What are Anonymous Inner Classes?
docs.text:
Created using object expressions.

window.addMouseListener(object : MouseAdapter() {
    override fun mouseClicked(e: MouseEvent) { ... }
})

docs.title: 38. What is SAM Conversion?
docs.text:
Single Abstract Method. Kotlin allows passing a lambda for a Java interface that has only one abstract method. Example: Runnable, Callable, OnClickListener.

button.setOnClickListener { view -> ... } // Lambda instead of object implementation

docs.title: 39. What is a Tail Recursive Function?
docs.text: A recursive function where the recursive call is the last operation performed. Marked with tailrec. The compiler optimizes this into a loop, preventing StackOverflowError.

docs.title: 40. What is a Functional Interface?
docs.text:
An interface with exactly one abstract method. Marked with fun interface.

fun interface IntPredicate {
    fun accept(i: Int): Boolean
}
val isEven = IntPredicate { it % 2 == 0 }

docs.title: 41. What are Coroutines?
docs.text: Coroutines are light-weight threads. They allow writing asynchronous code in a sequential manner. They are suspendable computations: they can suspend their execution without blocking the underlying thread.

docs.title: 42. Difference between launch and async.
docs.text: Feature launch async Return Returns a Job. Returns a Deferred<T>. Result Fire and forget. No result. Promise of a result later. Exception Crashes application if unhandled. Stored inside Deferred, thrown on .await().

docs.title: 43. What is runBlocking?
docs.text: It runs a new coroutine and blocks the current thread interruptibly until its completion. Use Case: Mainly for main functions and tests. Avoid in production UI code.

docs.title: 44. What is a Suspend Function?
docs.text: A function marked with suspend modifier. It can suspend the execution of a coroutine without blocking the thread. * Can only be called from a coroutine or another suspend function.

docs.title: 45. CoroutineScope vs CoroutineContext.
docs.text:
• CoroutineScope: Defines the scope for new coroutines. It manages the lifecycle (cancellation) of coroutines.
  • CoroutineContext: A set of elements that define the behavior of a coroutine (Job, Dispatcher, Name, ExceptionHandler).

docs.title: 46. Explain Dispatchers.
docs.text:
They determine which thread(s) the coroutine runs on.

  • Dispatchers.Main: UI thread (Android).
  • Dispatchers.IO: Optimized for disk/network IO (Thread pool).
  • Dispatchers.Default: Optimized for CPU-intensive work (Thread pool size = CPU cores).
  • Dispatchers.Unconfined: Starts in current thread, resumes in whatever thread called resume.

docs.title: 47. What is Job vs Deferred?
docs.text:
• Job: A handle to a background task with a lifecycle (Active, Cancelled, Completed).
  • Deferred: A generic subclass of Job that holds a result. It adds await() to retrieve the value.

docs.title: 48. What is Structured Concurrency?
docs.text: A paradigm where new coroutines can only be launched in a specific CoroutineScope. This ensures: 1. Children inherit context from parents. 2. Parent waits for all children to complete. 3. If parent is cancelled, all children are cancelled. 4. If a child fails, the parent (and other children) are cancelled.

docs.title: 49. How do you handle exceptions in Coroutines?
docs.text:
• try-catch: Inside the coroutine body.
  • CoroutineExceptionHandler: Context element to handle uncaught exceptions (only works on root coroutines launched with launch).
  • SupervisorJob / supervisorScope: Prevents failure propagation to the parent.

docs.title: 50. supervisorScope vs coroutineScope.
docs.text:
• coroutineScope: If one child fails, the scope fails and cancels all other children.
  • supervisorScope: If one child fails, it does not affect other children or the scope itself.

Diagram: Failure Propagation

graph TD
    A[Parent] --> B[Child 1 (Fails)]
    A --> C[Child 2]
    B -- "With coroutineScope" --> A
    A -- "Cancels" --> C
    B -- "With supervisorScope" --> X[Handled locally]
    A -. "Unaffected" .- C

docs.title: 51. What are Channels?
docs.text: Primitives for communication between coroutines. They provide a way to transfer a stream of values. * Logically similar to BlockingQueue. * Support send (suspend) and receive (suspend).

docs.title: 52. Explain Flow (Cold Stream) vs Channel (Hot Stream).
docs.text:
• Flow: Cold. Code inside flow { ... } does not run until collect() is called. Each collector gets its own execution.
  • Channel: Hot. Values are produced even if no one is listening.

docs.title: 53. StateFlow vs SharedFlow.
docs.text:
• StateFlow: A hot flow that holds state. Always has an initial value. Only emits the last known value to new collectors. (Replacement for LiveData).
  • SharedFlow: Highly configurable hot flow. Can emit events without state (no initial value). Can replay n values to new collectors.

docs.title: 54. What are buffer, conflate, and collectLatest?
docs.text:
• buffer(): Buffers emissions if collector is slow.
  • conflate(): Skips intermediate values if collector is slow, only processing the latest.
  • collectLatest(): Cancels the current block if a new value arrives.

docs.title: 55. How to handle Backpressure in Flows?
docs.text: Flows support backpressure by default because they use suspending functions. If the collector is slow, the emitter suspends.

docs.title: 56. Thread vs Coroutine?
docs.text:
• Thread: OS-managed resource. Expensive (~1MB stack). Context switching is costly.
  • Coroutine: User-space managed. Cheap (Objects). Thousands can run on one thread.

docs.title: 57. What is a Mutex?
docs.text: Mutual Exclusion. A locking primitive for coroutines. Unlike synchronized (which blocks the thread), Mutex.withLock suspends the coroutine.

docs.title: 58. What is an Actor?
docs.text: An entity made up of a coroutine, the state that is confined and encapsulated into this coroutine, and a channel to communicate with other coroutines. Note: The actor builder is currently obsolete in Kotlin Coroutines API favor of complex channels or other primitives, but the concept remains.

docs.title: 59. What is the select expression?
docs.text:
It waits for the result of multiple suspending functions simultaneously and selects the first one that becomes available.

select<Unit> {
    channelA.onReceive { ... }
    channelB.onReceive { ... }
}

docs.title: 60. How do you test Coroutines?
docs.text: Using kotlinx-coroutines-test library. * runTest: Replaces runBlocking for tests. Skips delays (virtual time). * StandardTestDispatcher: default for runTest. * UnconfinedTestDispatcher.

docs.title: 61. List vs MutableList.
docs.text:
• List<T>: Read-only interface. No add, remove, set.
  • MutableList<T>: Modifiable interface. Extends List.

docs.title: 62. map, filter, and reduce.
docs.text:
• map: Transforms each element.
  • filter: Returns elements matching a predicate.
  • reduce: Accumulates value starting with the first element.

docs.title: 63. What is flatMap?
docs.text:
Transforms each element into an Iterable and then flattens these iterables into a single list.

val list = listOf("abc", "def")
list.flatMap { it.toList() } // ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f']

docs.title: 64. What does zip do?
docs.text:
Combines two collections into a list of pairs.

val a = listOf(1, 2)
val b = listOf("A", "B")
a.zip(b) // [(1, "A"), (2, "B")]

docs.title: 65. Difference between fold and reduce.
docs.text:
• reduce: Uses the first element as the initial accumulator value. Throws exception on empty collection.
  • fold: Takes an explicit initial value. Works on empty collections.

docs.title: 66. Sequence vs Iterable (List).
docs.text:
• Iterable (List): Eager evaluation. Each step (map, filter) creates a new intermediate list.
  • Sequence: Lazy evaluation. Operations are vertical (element by element) rather than horizontal (step by step). No intermediate collections. Better for huge data sets.

docs.title: 67. How does groupBy work?
docs.text:
Returns a Map where keys are the grouping criteria and values are lists of original elements.

val words = listOf("a", "abc", "ab", "def", "abcd")
val byLength = words.groupBy { it.length }
// {1=[a], 3=[abc, def], 2=[ab], 4=[abcd]}

docs.title: 68. What is partition?
docs.text: Splits the collection into a pair of lists based on a predicate. * First list: Elements that match. * Second list: Elements that don't match.

docs.title: 69. any, all, and none.
docs.text:
• any: True if at least one matches.
  • all: True if all match.
  • none: True if no elements match.

docs.title: 70. What is associateBy?
docs.text: Creates a Map using elements as values and a key derived from the element. Risk: If keys are duplicates, the last one wins.

docs.title: 71. distinct vs toSet.
docs.text: Both return unique elements. * toSet(): Converts to a Set. * distinct(): Returns a List containing only distinct elements.

docs.title: 72. Arrays: IntArray vs Array<Int>.
docs.text:
• IntArray: Primitive int[] in JVM. Unboxed. Efficient.
  • Array<Int>: Object Integer[] in JVM. Boxed. More memory overhead.

docs.title: 73. String Manipulation.
docs.text: Strings are immutable. * trimMargin(): Removes whitespace. * split(): Returns List. * replace(): Returns new String.

docs.title: 74. Comparable vs Comparator.
docs.text:
• Comparable: Interface implemented by the class itself (compareTo). Defines natural order.
  • Comparator: External object that defines specific ordering (compare).

docs.title: 75. Why use the copy method in Data Classes?
docs.text: To create a new instance with some properties modified, while keeping others the same. Essential for immutability patterns.

docs.title: 76. Range iterators: until vs downTo.
docs.text:
• until: Excludes the end value. 1 until 10 (1..9).
  • downTo: Descending order. 10 downTo 1.

docs.title: 77. What is coerceIn?
docs.text:
Ensures a value is within a specific range.

val x = 15.coerceIn(0, 10) // Returns 10

docs.title: 78. How to measure execution time?
docs.text: measureTimeMillis { ... } or measureTime { ... } (requires kotlin.time).

docs.title: 79. How to generate Random numbers?
docs.text: Since Kotlin 1.3: Random.nextInt(from, until). Avoid java.util.Random in pure Kotlin code for multiplatform support.

docs.title: 80. Regular Expressions in Kotlin.
docs.text: Create using Regex("pattern"). * matchEntire() * find() * replace()

docs.title: 81. Explain JvmStatic, JvmOverloads, JvmField.
docs.text: Interoperability annotations. * @JvmStatic: Generates a real static method in the bytecode. * @JvmOverloads: Generates overloads for functions with default arguments. * @JvmField: Exposes a property as a public field (no getters/setters).

docs.title: 82. What is Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP)?
docs.text: A way to share code between platforms (Android, iOS, Web, Desktop). * Common code: Business logic. * Platform code: UI, Hardware access.

docs.title: 83. What is expect / actual mechanism?
docs.text: Used in KMP. * expect: Defined in common module. Declares "I need this functionality". * actual: Defined in platform modules (Android, iOS). Provides implementation.

docs.title: 84. Reflection in Kotlin.
docs.text: Inspects classes, properties, and functions at runtime. Requires kotlin-reflect.jar. Syntax: MyClass::class, ::myFunction.

docs.title: 85. KAPT vs KSP.
docs.text:
• KAPT: Kotlin Annotation Processing Tool. Runs Java annotation processors. Slow (generates Java stubs).
  • KSP: Kotlin Symbol Processing. Native to Kotlin. Faster.

docs.title: 86. Dependency Injection (Concept).
docs.text:
• Koin: Service Locator pattern (DSL). Pure Kotlin. No code generation. Runtime check.
  • Dagger/Hilt: Dependency Injection pattern. Compile-time generation. Strict.

docs.title: 87. What is ViewBinding?
docs.text: Generates a binding class for each XML layout file. Replaces findViewById. Null-safe and Type-safe.

docs.title: 88. What is Jetpack Compose?
docs.text: Modern toolkit for building native UI in Android using Kotlin. * Declarative: You describe the UI state, framework updates the view. * Functions: UI components are functions annotated with @Composable.

docs.title: 89. Memory Management (JVM).
docs.text: Kotlin on JVM uses the JVM Garbage Collector. * Heap: Objects. * Stack: Primitives, references.

docs.title: 90. What is a value class (Inline Class)?
docs.text:
Wraps a single value. At runtime, instances are represented by the underlying value (unboxed) where possible, avoiding object allocation.

@JvmInline
value class Password(val s: String)

docs.title: 91. What is Type Erasure?
docs.text: Generics are checked at compile time but removed (erased) at runtime. List<String> becomes just List (or raw List). Solution: Reified type parameters (inline functions).

docs.title: 92. Covariance and Contravariance (in vs out).
docs.text:
• out T (Covariant): Producer. Can only read T. Equivalent to ? extends T in Java. List<out Number> can hold List<Int>.
  • in T (Contravariant): Consumer. Can only write T. Equivalent to ? super T in Java. Comparable<in Number> can accept Double.

docs.title: 93. What is Star Projection *?
docs.text: Generic type with unknown argument. * MutableList<*>: Safe to read as Any?, but unsafe to write (except Nothing).

docs.title: 94. What is the Nothing type?
docs.text: A type that has no values. Represents "a value that never exists". * Used as return type for functions that always throw exceptions. * Subtype of all types.

docs.title: 95. What is the Unit type?
docs.text: Corresponds to void in Java. It is a real object (singleton).

docs.title: 96. What are Contracts?
docs.text: Let you describe the relationship between function parameters and return values/effects to the compiler. * Example: require(x != null) tells the compiler x is non-null afterwards.

docs.title: 97. What are Context Receivers?
docs.text:
(Experimental) Allows a function to have multiple receivers.

context(LoggingContext, DatabaseContext)
fun storeUser(user: User) { ... }

docs.title: 98. Kotlin Scripting (.kts).
docs.text: Kotlin code that can run as a script without compilation to a .jar. Used in Gradle Kotlin DSL.

docs.title: 99. Gradle Kotlin DSL.
docs.text: Writing build.gradle.kts using Kotlin instead of Groovy. * Pros: Autocomplete, Refactoring, Type safety. * Cons: Slower initial build (compilation).

docs.title: 100. What is the K2 Compiler?
docs.text:
The new Kotlin compiler frontend. * Faster compilation. * Better type inference. * Foundation for future language features.

End of Interview Questions

docs.title: Study Guide
docs.text:
To deepen your understanding of these concepts, check out the following resources:

  • Official Documentation: Kotlin Docs
  • Internal Style Guide: Kotlin Style Guide

docs.title: Protocol Buffers Interview Questions & Answers (100+)
docs.text:
What's on this page

  • Core content for this topic in the Inkorporated enterprise OS.
  • Practical guidance, roles, or standards as applicable.

What this enables

  • Consistent enterprise operations and decision-making.
  • Shared language for humans and cyborg AI agents.

This guide contains 100+ Protocol Buffers (Protobuf) interview questions, ranging from core concepts to advanced wire format encoding and gRPC integration. Each question includes a model answer and potential follow-up paths based on the candidate's response.

docs.title: 1. What is Protocol Buffers (Protobuf)?
docs.text:
Protocol Buffers is a language-neutral, platform-neutral, extensible mechanism for serializing structured data. It was developed by Google. You define how you want your data to be structured once (in .proto files), and then you can use generated source code to easily write and read your structured data to and from a variety of data streams and using a variety of languages.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Comparison with XML/JSON.
    • Follow-up: "Why would you choose it over JSON for a public REST API?"
    • Answer: You might not. JSON is better for human readability and browser consumption. Protobuf is better for internal microservices or performance-critical mobile clients.

docs.title: 2. Compare Protobuf vs. XML vs. JSON.
docs.text: Feature Protobuf JSON XML Format Binary Text (Human Readable) Text (Human Readable) Size Smallest Medium Largest Speed Fastest (Parsing/Serialization) Medium Slow Schema Required (.proto) Optional (JSON Schema) Optional (XSD) Typing Strong Loose Loose/Strong (with XSD)

docs.title: 3. What are the key benefits of using Protocol Buffers?
docs.text:
1. Performance: Smaller message size and faster processing (parsing/serialization) compared to text-based formats.
  2. Language Interoperability: Supports C++, Java, Python, Go, Ruby, C#, etc.
  3. Backward/Forward Compatibility: Fields can be added or removed without breaking old binaries.
  4. Schema Enforcement: The structure is defined and enforced by the compiler.

docs.title: 4. What is a .proto file?
docs.text:
It is a text file that contains the schema definition for the data structures (messages) and services. It uses the Protocol Buffers Interface Description Language (IDL).

syntax = "proto3";

message Person {
  string name = 1;
  int32 id = 2;
  string email = 3;
}

docs.title: 5. What are the main differences between proto2 and proto3?
docs.text:
• Field Presence: proto2 has required, optional, and repeated. proto3 removed required and optional (fields are optional by default and have default values).
  • Default Values: proto2 allows explicit default values (default = 5). proto3 uses zero values (0, empty string, false).
  • Enums: proto3 enums must start with a zero value (usually UNKNOWN).
  • Extensions: proto2 supports extensions. proto3 mostly replaced them with Any.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate complains about missing required.
    • Follow-up: "Why did Google remove required fields?"
    • Answer: Required fields harm backward compatibility. If a field stops being required in the logic but the schema says required, old consumers will crash if it's missing.

docs.title: 6. Why should you avoid required fields in proto2?
docs.text: If you ever wish to stop sending a required field, or if you want to rename it or effectively remove it, it becomes a breaking change. Any client reading the message that expects the field will fail to parse the message if it is missing. This makes evolving the schema extremely difficult.

docs.title: 7. What are "Tags" (Field Numbers) in Protobuf?
docs.text: Each field in the message definition has a unique numbered tag (e.g., string name = 1;). * These numbers are used to identify fields in the binary message wire format. * They must not change once your message type is in use.

docs.title: 8. Why are field numbers 1 through 15 more efficient?
docs.text: Field numbers 1-15 take one byte to encode (including the field number and wire type). Field numbers 16-2047 take two bytes. * Optimization Tip: Use 1-15 for very frequently occurring fields.

docs.title: 9. What basic data types are supported in Protobuf?
docs.text:
• Integers: int32, int64, uint32, uint64, sint32, sint64 (signed), fixed32, fixed64.
  • Floating Point: float, double.
  • Boolean: bool.
  • Strings: string (UTF-8), bytes (arbitrary byte arrays).

docs.title: 10. How does Protobuf handle Backward Compatibility?
docs.text:
• New Fields: Old code reads new data -> It ignores (or stores as unknown) the new fields.
  • Deleted Fields: Old code reads data missing the deleted field -> It sees the default value.
  • Rule: Never reuse a field tag number.

docs.title: 11. What is the generated code?
docs.text: The protoc compiler generates classes for your specific language (e.g., Person.java, person_pb2.py). * These classes provide builders, accessors (getters/setters), and methods to serialize/parse (toByteArray(), parseFrom()).

docs.title: 12. Can you modify a field's type without breaking compatibility?
docs.text: Generally No, with exceptions: * int32, uint32, int64, uint64, and bool are compatible (can be changed to each other, though values might be truncated). * string and bytes are compatible if the bytes are valid UTF-8. * Changing int32 to string will break parsing.

docs.title: 13. What is the repeated keyword?
docs.text:
It indicates that the field can be repeated any number of times (including zero). It is dynamically sized, similar to a List or Array. 

repeated string phone_numbers = 4;

docs.title: 14. What are "Unknown Fields"?
docs.text: Fields present in the parsed data that the parser does not recognize (e.g., from a newer version of the schema). * Proto2: Preserved in the message and re-serialized. * Proto3 (Early): Discarded. * Proto3 (Modern): Preserved (since version 3.5+).

docs.title: 15. Is Protobuf self-describing?
docs.text: No. Unlike XML or JSON, a Protobuf binary message does not contain field names, only tag numbers. You must have the .proto definition (schema) to decode the data meaningfully.

docs.title: 16. What is the default value for an int32 field in Proto3?
docs.text: 0. * There is no distinction between "0 was explicitly set" and "the field was missing" in the wire format (for scalar types in Proto3).

docs.title: 17. How do you distinguish between missing field and default value in Proto3?
docs.text: For scalar types (int, bool), you cannot by default. * Solution: Use wrapper types (e.g., google.protobuf.Int32Value) or the optional keyword (available in newer Proto3) which generates a presence bit.

docs.title: 18. What is the syntax statement?
docs.text: The first non-empty, non-comment line of the .proto file. * syntax = "proto3"; * If omitted, the compiler assumes proto2.

docs.title: 19. Can you comment in .proto files?
docs.text: Yes. * // Single line comment * /* Multi-line comment */

docs.title: 20. How are bytes different from string?
docs.text:
• string: Must contain valid UTF-8 text.
  • bytes: Can contain arbitrary binary data (e.g., an image, an encrypted payload).

docs.title: 21. How do you define a package?
docs.text:
package tutorial;
* Helps prevent name clashes between different projects. * In Java, creates a package directory structure (unless java_package option is used). * In C++, generates a namespace.

docs.title: 22. What are imports in Protobuf?
docs.text:
Used to use definitions from other .proto files. 

import "google/protobuf/timestamp.proto";

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Public Imports.
    • Follow-up: "What does import public do?"
    • Answer: It forwards the import. Any file importing the current file also gets the transitive public imports.

docs.title: 23. Explain "Nested Types".
docs.text:
You can define a message inside another message. 

message SearchResponse {
  message Result {
    string url = 1;
  }
  repeated Result results = 1;
}
* Referenced outside as SearchResponse.Result.

docs.title: 24. How do you define an Enum?
docs.text:
enum Corpus {
  CORPUS_UNSPECIFIED = 0; // Proto3 requires 0 value
  CORPUS_UNIVERSAL = 1;
  CORPUS_WEB = 2;
}

docs.title: 25. Can Enums share values (Aliases)?
docs.text:
Yes, if you set the allow_alias option. 

enum EnumAllowingAlias {
  option allow_alias = true;
  UNKNOWN = 0;
  STARTED = 1;
  RUNNING = 1; // Alias to STARTED
}

docs.title: 26. What is a map in Protobuf?
docs.text:
Associative arrays (key-value pairs). 

map<string, Project> projects = 3;
* Keys: integers, bools, strings. (No floats, no enums). * Values: Any type except another map. * On the wire, maps are equivalent to a repeated message containing key and value fields.

docs.title: 27. What is oneof?
docs.text:
A set of fields where only one can be set at a time. Setting one field clears the others. Saves memory. 

message Profile {
  oneof avatar {
    string image_url = 1;
    bytes image_data = 2;
  }
}

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Repeated in oneof.
    • Follow-up: "Can you have repeated fields inside a oneof?"
    • Answer: No.

docs.title: 28. What are reserved fields?
docs.text:
If you delete a field, you should reserve its tag number (and name) to prevent future users from accidentally reusing it and causing corruption with old data. 

message Foo {
  reserved 2, 15, 9 to 11;
  reserved "foo", "bar";
}

docs.title: 29. What happens if you define two fields with the same tag number?
docs.text: The protoc compiler will throw an error and fail to generate code. Tags must be unique within a message.

docs.title: 30. What is java_multiple_files option?
docs.text:
option java_multiple_files = true;
* False (Default): Generates a single outer class containing all messages as inner static classes. * True: Generates separate .java files for each message/enum. Better for large projects.

docs.title: 31. What is the deprecated option?
docs.text:
int32 old_field = 1 [deprecated = true];
* Marks the field as deprecated. Generated code will often have annotations (like @Deprecated in Java) to warn developers.

docs.title: 32. How do you handle Date and Time in Protobuf?
docs.text:
Do not use string (e.g., ISO-8601) or int64 (seconds) directly if you want standard interoperability. Use Well Known Types: 

import "google/protobuf/timestamp.proto";
// ...
google.protobuf.Timestamp last_updated = 1;

docs.title: 33. What is the Any type?
docs.text:
Allows you to embed a message without having its .proto definition at compile time. 

import "google/protobuf/any.proto";
message ErrorStatus {
  string message = 1;
  repeated google.protobuf.Any details = 2;
}
* Internally stores the byte data and a Type URL string.

docs.title: 34. How do you define a Service in Protobuf?
docs.text:
Used for RPC (Remote Procedure Call) systems like gRPC. 

service SearchService {
  rpc Search (SearchRequest) returns (SearchResponse);
}

docs.title: 35. Can a field be both repeated and optional?
docs.text: In proto3, repeated implies a list (0 to N). optional implies presence tracking (0 or 1). They are mutually exclusive.

docs.title: 36. What is the best practice for naming fields?
docs.text:
• Field Names: snake_case (e.g., song_name).
  • Message Names: CamelCase (e.g., SongRequest).
  • Enums: CAPS_WITH_UNDERSCORES.
  • Reason: The generated code converts these to the language-specific standard (e.g., getSongName() in Java, SongName property in C#).

docs.title: 37. Can you default a map field?
docs.text: No. Map fields cannot have default values explicitly defined, and they are never null (an empty map is the default).

docs.title: 38. How to update an Enum?
docs.text:
• You can add new values.
  • Be careful: If an old client receives a new enum value it doesn't know, it treats it as an unknown integer value (in Proto3) or discards it (in older Proto2).
  • Always preserve the numeric values.

docs.title: 39. What is a "wrapper type"?
docs.text: Types in google/protobuf/wrappers.proto (e.g., StringValue, Int32Value). * They wrap primitives in a Message. * Allows distinction between "null" (message not present) and default value (0 or "").

docs.title: 40. Can you inherit from other messages?
docs.text: No. Protobuf does not support inheritance. You must use Composition (nesting messages).

docs.title: 41. Explain Base 128 Varints.
docs.text: Variable-length integers. * Uses 1 byte for small numbers, more bytes for large numbers. * The MSB (Most Significant Bit) of each byte indicates if there are more bytes to follow (1 = yes, 0 = last byte). * Example: The number 1 is 0000 0001. The number 300 takes two bytes.

docs.title: 42. How is a field encoded (Key-Value)?
docs.text: A field in the stream is a Key followed by a Value. * Key = (field_number << 3) | wire_type. * The last 3 bits store the wire type.

docs.title: 43. What are the Wire Types?
docs.text: Type Name Meaning Used For 0 Varint Variable length int32, int64, bool, enum 1 64-bit Fixed 8 bytes fixed64, double 2 Length-delimited Length + Bytes string, bytes, messages, packed repeated 3 Start Group (Deprecated) Groups (Proto2) 4 End Group (Deprecated) Groups (Proto2) 5 32-bit Fixed 4 bytes fixed32, float

docs.title: 44. Why does int32 encode negative numbers inefficiently?
docs.text: In standard Varint encoding, negative numbers are sign-extended to 64 bits (even for int32), resulting in 10 bytes on the wire.

docs.title: 45. What is ZigZag Encoding?
docs.text: Used by sint32 and sint64 types. * It maps signed integers to unsigned integers so that small absolute values (like -1, -2) become small unsigned values. * -1 -> 1, 1 -> 2, -2 -> 3. * Makes encoding negative numbers efficient.

docs.title: 46. What is the difference between int32 and sint32?
docs.text:
• int32: Uses standard Varint. Good for positive numbers. Bad for negative (always 10 bytes).
  • sint32: Uses ZigZag Varint. Good for mixed positive/negative numbers.

docs.title: 47. How are Strings encoded?
docs.text: Wire Type 2 (Length-delimited). Format: [Tag] [Length Varint] [UTF-8 Bytes].

docs.title: 48. How are nested messages encoded?
docs.text: Also Wire Type 2. * The value is simply the serialized byte stream of the inner message. * Allows "lazy parsing" (decoding the outer message without parsing the inner one immediately).

docs.title: 49. What is "Packed Encoding"?
docs.text: Used for repeated fields of scalar numeric types (proto3 default). * Unpacked: [Tag][Value] [Tag][Value] [Tag][Value] (Repeats Tag overhead). * Packed: [Tag][Length][Value][Value][Value] (Tag appears once). Saves space.

docs.title: 50. How does a decoder know when a message ends?
docs.text:
It doesn't. * Protobuf messages are not self-delimiting. * If you write multiple messages to a single file/stream, you must implement a framing protocol (e.g., write the length of the message before the message itself).

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Use writeDelimitedTo.
    • Follow-up: "Is that standard across languages?"
    • Answer: Most Java/C++ libs support it, but it's not strictly part of the wire format spec, just a common utility.

docs.title: 51. Is the wire format order deterministic?
docs.text: No. * Fields can appear in any order. * Unknown fields might be interspersed. * Maps have no defined order. * Implication: You cannot compare two binary blobs for equality to check if messages are equal. You must parse and compare.

docs.title: 52. What is Canonical Encoding?
docs.text: A deterministic serialization approach (e.g., sorting map keys, sorting field tags) sometimes used for hashing signatures, but standard Protobuf libraries do not guarantee this by default.

docs.title: 53. How much space does a boolean take?
docs.text:
• 1 Byte for the tag (if field number < 16).
  • 1 Byte for the value (0 or 1).
  • Total: 2 Bytes.

docs.title: 54. Can you decode a proto3 message using a proto2 schema?
docs.text: Partially. The wire format is mostly compatible. * Proto3 specific types (like Map or Packed repeated fields) might cause issues if the Proto2 schema doesn't define them correctly (though packed=true exists in proto2). * Missing required fields in the input (from proto3 source) will cause proto2 parsers to fail.

docs.title: 55. What happens if the wire type doesn't match the schema?
docs.text: The parser generally throws an exception or marks it as a parse error. * Example: Expecting Varint (Type 0) but finding Length-delimited (Type 2).

docs.title: 56. How is fixed32 different from int32 on the wire?
docs.text:
• int32: Varint encoded (1-5 bytes typically).
  • fixed32: Always 4 bytes.
  • Use Case: fixed32 is better if values are usually very large (random IDs, hashes) where Varint would take 5 bytes.

docs.title: 57. How do Maps look on the wire?
docs.text:
A map map<K, V> field = N is serialized as a repeated message of a virtual entry message: 

message MapEntry {
  K key = 1;
  V value = 2;
}
repeated MapEntry field = N;

docs.title: 58. What is the limit on message size?
docs.text:
• Theoretical: 2GB (due to signed 32-bit integer limits in many implementations like Java/C++).
  • Practical: Default limits are often set to 64MB to prevent DOS attacks (OOM). Can be increased via API.

docs.title: 59. Does Protobuf compress data?
docs.text: No. It uses efficient binary encoding (removing whitespace, using varints), which results in small sizes, but it does not use compression algorithms like GZIP or LZW. * Tip: You can GZIP the resulting binary protobuf for further reduction.

docs.title: 60. How does field reordering affect the wire format?
docs.text: It doesn't. * If you change the order of fields in the .proto file (e.g., move id = 1 below name = 2), the wire format depends only on the Tag Number, not the line number in the file.

docs.title: 61. What is protoc?
docs.text: The Protocol Buffer Compiler. * Input: .proto files. * Output: Generated code (C++, Java, Python, etc.).

docs.title: 62. How do you compile a python file?
docs.text: protoc --python_out=. my_proto.proto

docs.title: 63. What is a "Builder" in Java generated code?
docs.text:
Protobuf messages in Java are Immutable. * To create or modify a message, you must use the generated Builder class. 

Person p = Person.newBuilder().setName("Jules").build();

docs.title: 64. How do you merge two messages?
docs.text:
Builders support merging. 

builder.mergeFrom(otherMessage);
* Singular fields: Overwritten by otherMessage. * Repeated fields: Concatenated.

docs.title: 65. Does Protobuf support inheritance in generated code?
docs.text: No. * Generated classes extend GeneratedMessageV3. * They do not support extending your own custom classes to add logic. * Reason: Preserves the "Data Object" nature and serialization guarantees.

docs.title: 66. How to print a message for debugging?
docs.text:
• toString(): Returns a human-readable text format representation.
  • Do not use this for parsing/serialization logic, only for logging.

docs.title: 67. Can you convert Protobuf to JSON?
docs.text: Yes. JsonFormat (Java) or MessageToJson (Python) util classes are provided by the library. * It converts field names to JSON keys. * It handles Enums as strings.

docs.title: 68. What is protoc-gen-go?
docs.text: The plugin for Go language support. protoc itself doesn't support Go natively out of the box in the main binary; it delegates to this plugin.

docs.title: 69. How does Python dynamic nature affect Protobuf?
docs.text: Python code generated by protoc is often just descriptors. The actual message classes are created dynamically at runtime (metaclasses) in newer versions, using C++ extensions for speed.

docs.title: 70. What is the option optimize_for?
docs.text:
option optimize_for = CODE_SIZE;
* SPEED (Default): Generates optimized code for serializing/parsing. Larger class files. * CODE_SIZE: Generates minimal classes that rely on shared reflection-based code. Slower, but smaller binary. * LITE_RUNTIME: Generates classes that only depend on the "Lite" library (no descriptors/reflection). Good for mobile.

docs.title: 71. How do you check if a field is set in Proto3 (Java)?
docs.text:
• Message fields: hasField().
  • Scalar fields: You can't (unless using optional keyword). You only check if value != 0.

docs.title: 72. What are "Well Known Types"?
docs.text: A set of .proto definitions provided by Google that cover common use cases. * Timestamp, Duration * StringValue, BoolValue (Wrappers) * FieldMask * Struct (JSON Object)

docs.title: 73. What is FieldMask?
docs.text: Used in Update/Patch RPCs. * Lists which fields the client wants to update. * Allows distinct updates (e.g., update only 'email', leave 'name' alone) even if the object has both.

docs.title: 74. How does reflection work in Protobuf?
docs.text: You can traverse a message without knowing its type at compile time. * Descriptors: Describe the schema (MessageDescriptor, FieldDescriptor). * Reflection Interface: Get value by FieldDescriptor.

docs.title: 75. How to write a custom protoc plugin?
docs.text: A plugin is an executable that accepts a CodeGeneratorRequest (protobuf message) from standard input and writes a CodeGeneratorResponse to standard output. * Can be written in any language (Python/Go are popular).

docs.title: 76. What is Struct type?
docs.text: google.protobuf.Struct. * Represents a dynamic JSON object. * Maps strings to Value (which can be number, string, list, struct, etc.). * Useful when data structure is not known at compile time (loss of type safety).

docs.title: 77. Handling Polymorphism?
docs.text: Since there is no inheritance, use: 1. Oneof: If types are known. 2. Any: If types are open-ended.

docs.title: 78. What is DescriptorSet?
docs.text: A file containing the parsed schema information (descriptors) of .proto files. * Generated via protoc --descriptor_set_out=file.pb. * Used by tools (like grpcurl) to understand messages without source code.

docs.title: 79. How to handle huge messages?
docs.text: Protobuf loads the entire message into memory. * Solution: Don't use a single huge message. Use a stream of smaller messages or split data into chunks.

docs.title: 80. Dependency Management?
docs.text: protoc needs import paths (-I or --proto_path). * Complex projects use tools like Buf to manage dependencies and linting.

docs.title: 81. How does gRPC relate to Protobuf?
docs.text: gRPC is an RPC framework. Protobuf is the default: 1. IDL: Defines the service and messages. 2. Serialization: Encodes the payload on the wire.

docs.title: 82. Can gRPC use JSON?
docs.text: Yes, but it's not the default. You can use gRPC-Web or custom codecs, but you lose the performance benefits of Protobuf.

docs.title: 83. What are the 4 types of gRPC methods?
docs.text:
1. Unary: Simple Request -> Response.
  2. Server Streaming: Request -> Stream of Responses.
  3. Client Streaming: Stream of Requests -> Response.
  4. Bidirectional Streaming: Stream -> Stream (Async).

docs.title: 84. Why is Protobuf faster than JSON?
docs.text:
1. Size: Binary is compact (Varints, no field names). Less bandwidth.
  2. Parsing: CPU efficient. No text scanning/tokenizing. It's mostly reading bytes and jumping pointers.

docs.title: 85. What is "Zero-Copy" parsing?
docs.text: Some C++ implementations (like StringPiece or Cord) allow the protobuf parser to point directly to the raw byte buffer for string/byte fields instead of copying memory.

docs.title: 86. How to validate Protobuf messages?
docs.text:
Protobuf ensures type safety, not value validity (e.g., email format, age > 0). * Solution: Use PGV (Protoc Gen Validate). Annotate fields in .proto: 

string email = 1 [(validate.rules).string.email = true];

docs.title: 87. What is Schema Registry?
docs.text: In systems like Kafka, a Schema Registry stores the .proto definitions (versioned). * Producers send ID + Binary Data. * Consumers fetch Schema by ID to decode. * Decouples producers and consumers.

docs.title: 88. Protobuf Text Format vs JSON?
docs.text: Protobuf has its own text format (looks like the .proto default values). * name: "Jules" id: 42 * Used for config files or debugging. Not valid JSON.

docs.title: 89. How to handle breaking changes safely?
docs.text:
1. Create a new field string name_v2 = 5;.
  2. Deprecate old field name.
  3. Dual-write to both in application logic.
  4. Migrate readers to name_v2.
  5. Stop writing name.

docs.title: 90. What is Arena Allocation (C++)?
docs.text: A memory management optimization. * Allocates a large block of memory (Arena) upfront. * All message objects are allocated from this block. * Freeing the Arena frees everything at once. * Reduces malloc/free overhead and improves cache locality.

docs.title: 91. Explain "Unknown Fields" attack vector.
docs.text: If a server acts as a proxy (Read -> Modify -> Write), and it preserves unknown fields: * Attacker sends a malicious payload in an "unknown field". * Server verifies known fields (checks pass). * Server forwards message to a vulnerable internal service that does understand the field.

docs.title: 92. Deterministic Serialization options.
docs.text: Required for things like hashing a message to sign it. * Proto3 C++ has MessageDifferencer and serialization options to force map sorting. * Generally, don't rely on binary equality.

docs.title: 93. Is Protobuf encrypted?
docs.text: No. It is just an encoding format. If you need security, you must encrypt the transport (TLS/SSL) or the payload field (bytes encrypted_data = 1).

docs.title: 94. Comparison with FlatBuffers?
docs.text: Feature Protobuf FlatBuffers Parsing Decoding step required (unpack to object). No parsing (Zero-copy access). Memory Allocates objects. Reads directly from buffer. Use Case Microservices, Storage. Games, Real-time (no GC/alloc overhead).

docs.title: 95. Comparison with Apache Avro?
docs.text: Feature Protobuf Avro Schema Explicitly generated code. Schema stored with data (usually). Ecosystem Google/Microservices/gRPC. Hadoop/Big Data/Kafka. Evolution Tag numbers. Schema resolution rules.

docs.title: 96. What is the files field in FileDescriptorSet?
docs.text: It contains a list of FileDescriptorProto messages, representing the parsed content of each .proto file (including dependencies).

docs.title: 97. How to exclude a field from JSON output?
docs.text: Use json_name option? No, usually fields are included. * Some JSON Printers have options to printingDefaultValues or ignoringUnknownFields. * To hide it, you might need a separate "DTO" proto.

docs.title: 98. Custom Options?
docs.text:
You can define your own options to annotate files, messages, or fields. 

extend google.protobuf.FieldOptions {
  bool my_option = 50000;
}
string name = 1 [(my_option) = true];
* Access these via Reflection at runtime.

docs.title: 99. Performance: String vs Bytes?
docs.text:
• string requires UTF-8 validation during parsing and serialization.
  • bytes is raw copy.
  • If you have ASCII data or don't care about encoding validation, bytes is slightly faster.

docs.title: 100. Naming convention for repeated fields?
docs.text:
Usually plural. * repeated string phone_numbers = 1; * Generated Java: getPhoneNumbersList(), getPhoneNumbers(index).

End of Interview Questions

docs.title: Study Guide
docs.text:
To deepen your understanding of these concepts, check out the following resources:

  • Official Documentation: Protocol Buffers Docs

docs.title: Python Interview Questions & Answers (100+)
docs.text:
What's on this page

  • Core content for this topic in the Inkorporated enterprise OS.
  • Practical guidance, roles, or standards as applicable.

What this enables

  • Consistent enterprise operations and decision-making.
  • Shared language for humans and cyborg AI agents.

This guide contains 100+ Python interview questions, ranging from basic to advanced. Each question includes a model answer, code snippets, and potential follow-up paths based on the candidate's response.

docs.title: 1. What is the difference between list and tuple?
docs.text:
Feature List Tuple Mutability Mutable (can change) Immutable (cannot change) Syntax [] () Performance Slower (overhead for resizing) Faster (fixed size) Use Case Collections of items that change Constant data, Dictionary keys

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate mentions Mutability.

    • Follow-up: "Can a tuple contain a mutable object (like a list) and can that object be modified?"
    • Answer: Yes. t = (1, [2, 3]). You can modify t[1] because the tuple only stores the reference to the list, which doesn't change, even if the list content does.

  • Path B: Candidate focuses on Syntax.

    • Follow-up: "How do you create a tuple with a single element?"
    • Answer: You must use a trailing comma: t = (1,). Without it, Python interprets it as an integer in parentheses (1).

docs.title: 2. How is memory managed in Python?
docs.text:
Python uses a private heap containing all Python objects and data structures. The management of this private heap is ensured internally by the Python Memory Manager.

Key mechanisms: 1. Reference Counting: Objects are deallocated when their reference count drops to zero. 2. Garbage Collection: Handles cyclic references that reference counting cannot catch.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate mentions Garbage Collection (GC).
    • Follow-up: "When does the Garbage Collector run?"
    • Answer: It runs periodically based on thresholds (generations 0, 1, 2). It can also be triggered manually using gc.collect().

docs.title: 3. What is PEP 8?
docs.text:
PEP 8 is the style guide for Python code. It ensures consistency and readability. Key rules: * Indentation: 4 spaces. * Line Length: 79 characters. * Variable Names: snake_case for functions/variables, CamelCase for classes.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate is familiar.
    • Follow-up: "How do you check your code against PEP 8 automatically?"
    • Answer: Using linters like flake8, pylint, or formatters like black (which is opinionated but compliant).

docs.title: 4. What are the key features of Python?
docs.text:
• Interpreted: Executed line by line.
  • Dynamically Typed: Type checks happen at runtime.
  • Object-Oriented: Everything is an object.
  • High-level: Abstraction from memory details.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate mentions 'Dynamically Typed'.
    • Follow-up: "What is the difference between dynamic typing and strong typing? Is Python strongly typed?"
    • Answer: Yes, Python is strongly typed. You cannot add "1" (string) and 1 (int) without explicit conversion, unlike JavaScript (weakly typed).

docs.title: 5. Explain is vs ==.
docs.text:
• ==: Checks for Value Equality (do they hold the same data?).
  • is: Checks for Reference Equality (do they point to the exact same memory address?).
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]
print(a == b) # True
print(a is b) # False (different objects)

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate understands the difference.
    • Follow-up: "Why is None usually compared using is?"
    • Answer: Because None is a singleton. There is only one instance of None in the system, so is is faster and safer (prevents custom __eq__ methods from fooling the check).

docs.title: 6. What acts as a placeholder for an empty block?
docs.text: The pass statement. It is a null operation; nothing happens when it executes. Useful for empty function definitions or loops during development.

docs.title: 7. What is a Dictionary?
docs.text:
A collection of Key-Value pairs. It is unordered (before Python 3.7), mutable, and indexed. Keys must be immutable (hashable).

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate mentions Hashable keys.
    • Follow-up: "Can I use a list as a dictionary key?"
    • Answer: No, lists are mutable and thus not hashable. You can use a tuple as a key if it contains only immutable elements.

docs.title: 8. How do you copy an object in Python?
docs.text:
• Assignment (=): Creates a new reference to the same object.
  • Shallow Copy (copy.copy() or [:]): Creates a new object, but inserts references into it to the objects found in the original.
  • Deep Copy (copy.deepcopy()): Creates a new object and recursively copies everything.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate explains Shallow Copy.
    • Follow-up: "If I change a nested list in a shallow copy, does it affect the original?"
    • Answer: Yes, because the inner list reference is shared.

docs.title: 9. What is a set?
docs.text: Unordered collection of unique elements. Useful for: * Removing duplicates. * Set operations (Union |, Intersection &, Difference -).

docs.title: 10. How do you manage packages in Python?
docs.text:
Using pip (Python Installer Package). Files usually listed in requirements.txt or pyproject.toml.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate mentions Virtual Environments.
    • Follow-up: "Why are virtual environments important?"
    • Answer: To isolate dependencies per project, avoiding version conflicts between projects or with the system Python.

docs.title: 11. What is the difference between .py and .pyc files?
docs.text:
• .py: Source code.
  • .pyc: Bytecode (compiled version). Python compiles .py to .pyc to speed up loading. Stored in __pycache__.

docs.title: 12. Explain String Interpolation methods.
docs.text:
1. % formatting (Old): "Hello %s" % name
  2. .format() (Newer): "Hello {}".format(name)
  3. f-Strings (Modern, Python 3.6+): f"Hello {name}" (Fastest and most readable).

docs.title: 13. What is the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL)?
docs.text:
A mutex that protects access to Python objects, preventing multiple native threads from executing Python bytecodes at once. This means Python threads are not truly parallel on multi-core CPUs for CPU-bound tasks.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate says 'Python cannot do parallelism'.
    • Follow-up: "How do we achieve parallelism then?"
    • Answer: Use multiprocessing (separate processes have their own memory/GIL) or use libraries like NumPy that release the GIL for heavy computations.

docs.title: 14. What are negative indexes?
docs.text: Python allows accessing elements from the end of a sequence using negative numbers. -1 is the last item, -2 is the second to last.

docs.title: 15. What is slicing?
docs.text:
Extracting a part of a sequence. Syntax: object[start:stop:step]

a = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print(a[::-1]) # [5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0] (Reverses list)

docs.title: 16. What is the difference between range and xrange?
docs.text:
• Python 2: range returned a list, xrange returned an iterator (memory efficient).
  • Python 3: xrange is gone. range now behaves like the old xrange (returns a range object/iterator).

docs.title: 17. How do you handle errors in Python?
docs.text:
Using try, except, else, and finally.

try:
    x = 1 / 0
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("Error")
else:
    print("Success") # Runs if no exception
finally:
    print("Cleanup") # Always runs

docs.title: 18. What is a Docstring?
docs.text:
A string literal that occurs as the first statement in a module, function, class, or method definition. Accessed via __doc__.

Style: Triple quotes """Description""".

docs.title: 19. What is __init__?
docs.text: The constructor method for a class. It is automatically called when a new instance of the class is created. Used to initialize attributes.

docs.title: 20. What is self?
docs.text: It represents the instance of the class. By using self, we can access the attributes and methods of the class in Python. It is an explicit first argument (unlike this in Java/C++ which is implicit).

docs.title: 21. What is the difference between break, continue, and pass?
docs.text: Statement Effect break Terminates the loop immediately. continue Skips the current iteration and jumps to the next. pass Does nothing (placeholder).

docs.title: 22. Can you have an else clause with a loop?
docs.text:
Yes, else in a loop executes when the loop completes normally (without encountering a break statement).

for i in range(3):
    print(i)
else:
    print("Done") # Prints "Done"

for i in range(3):
    if i == 1:
        break
else:
    print("Done") # Does NOT print

docs.title: 23. What are iterators and iterables?
docs.text:
• Iterable: An object capable of returning its members one at a time (e.g., list, string). Has __iter__().
  • Iterator: An object representing a stream of data. Has __next__() and __iter__().

docs.title: 24. What is List Comprehension?
docs.text:
A concise way to create lists. Syntax: [expression for item in iterable if condition]

squares = [x**2 for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]

docs.title: 25. What is the ternary operator in Python?
docs.text:
[on_true] if [expression] else [on_false]

x = 10
status = "Even" if x % 2 == 0 else "Odd"

docs.title: 26. How does enumerate() work?
docs.text:
It adds a counter to an iterable and returns it as an enumerate object (iterator of tuples).

names = ["Alice", "Bob"]
for index, name in enumerate(names, start=1):
    print(f"{index}: {name}")
# Output:
# 1: Alice
# 2: Bob

docs.title: 27. What is zip()?
docs.text:
Aggregates elements from two or more iterables. Returns an iterator of tuples.

names = ["Alice", "Bob"]
ages = [25, 30]
print(list(zip(names, ages))) # [('Alice', 25), ('Bob', 30)]

docs.title: 28. What happens if zipped lists are different lengths?
docs.text: zip() stops at the shortest list. To fill missing values, use itertools.zip_longest().

docs.title: 29. How do you swap two variables in one line?
docs.text: a, b = b, a

docs.title: 30. What is the with statement?
docs.text:
It is used for Context Management. It ensures that resources (like file streams) are properly cleaned up (closed) even if exceptions occur.

with open('file.txt', 'r') as f:
    content = f.read()
# f is automatically closed here

docs.title: 31. Explain the if __name__ == "__main__": block.
docs.text: It checks if the script is being run directly (not imported as a module). If imported, __name__ is the module name; if run directly, __name__ is "__main__".

docs.title: 32. What is dict.get() vs dict[]?
docs.text:
• dict[key]: Raises KeyError if key is missing.
  • dict.get(key, default): Returns None (or specified default) if key is missing. Safer.

docs.title: 33. How to check if a key exists in a dictionary?
docs.text:
Use the in operator. 

if "key" in my_dict:
    print("Exists")

docs.title: 34. What is the difference between for loop and while loop?
docs.text:
• for: Iterates over a sequence (known number of times).
  • while: Repeats as long as a condition is true (unknown number of times).

docs.title: 35. How to flatten a list of lists?
docs.text:
Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: List Comprehension. 
    flat = [item for sublist in l for item in sublist]
  • Path B: itertools.chain. 
    import itertools
flat = list(itertools.chain(*l))

docs.title: 36. What is the difference between *args and **kwargs?
docs.text:
• *args: Allows passing a variable number of positional arguments (tuple).
  • **kwargs: Allows passing a variable number of keyword arguments (dictionary).
def func(*args, **kwargs):
    print(args)   # (1, 2)
    print(kwargs) # {'a': 3}

func(1, 2, a=3)

docs.title: 37. What are lambda functions?
docs.text:
Anonymous, small functions defined with the lambda keyword. They can have any number of arguments but only one expression.

add = lambda x, y: x + y
print(add(2, 3)) # 5
