docs.title: 38. Explain map(), filter(), and reduce().
docs.text:
• map(func, iter): Applies func to all items in iter.
  • filter(func, iter): Creates a list of elements for which func returns true.
  • reduce(func, iter): Applies a rolling computation to sequential pairs of values (requires functools).

docs.title: 39. What is a "First Class Function"?
docs.text: Functions are treated like any other variable. They can be: 1. Passed as arguments to other functions. 2. Returned from other functions. 3. Assigned to variables.

docs.title: 40. What is Scope Resolution (LEGB Rule)?
docs.text: Python searches for variables in this order: 1. Local (Inside function) 2. Enclosing (Nested function globals) 3. Global (Module level) 4. Built-in (Python keywords)

docs.title: 41. What is a Closure?
docs.text:
A function object that remembers values in enclosing scopes even if they are not present in memory.

def outer(x):
    def inner(y):
        return x + y # Remembers x
    return inner

add5 = outer(5)
print(add5(10)) # 15

docs.title: 42. What is the global keyword?
docs.text:
Allows you to modify a global variable inside a local scope (function).

x = 10
def change():
    global x
    x = 20

docs.title: 43. What is the nonlocal keyword?
docs.text: Allows you to modify a variable in the nearest enclosing scope (not global). Used in nested functions.

docs.title: 44. Default Argument Values Gotcha.
docs.text:
Question: What is the output? 

def extend_list(val, list=[]):
    list.append(val)
    return list

list1 = extend_list(10)
list2 = extend_list(123, [])
list3 = extend_list('a')
print(list1)
print(list3)
Answer: [10, 'a'] and [10, 'a']. Default arguments are evaluated once at function definition time, so the list is shared across calls.

docs.title: 45. What is Currying?
docs.text: Decomposing a function that takes multiple arguments into a sequence of functions that each take a single argument. (Not native to Python syntax but achievable with closures or functools.partial).

docs.title: 46. What is a Higher-Order Function?
docs.text: A function that takes another function as an argument or returns a function. (e.g., map, decorator).

docs.title: 47. Difference between parameters and arguments?
docs.text:
• Parameters: Variables listed in the function definition.
  • Arguments: Actual values passed to the function when called.

docs.title: 48. Can you force Keyword-Only arguments?
docs.text:
Yes, by placing a * in the parameter list.

def func(a, *, b):
    pass

func(1, b=2) # OK
func(1, 2)   # Error

docs.title: 49. What is introspection (or reflection)?
docs.text: The ability of a program to examine the type or properties of an object at runtime. Examples: type(), id(), dir(), getattr(), hasattr().

docs.title: 50. How to create a function generator?
docs.text:
Use the yield keyword instead of return.

def count_up_to(n):
    count = 1
    while count <= n:
        yield count
        count += 1

docs.title: 51. What is the time complexity of looking up a key in a Dictionary?
docs.text: O(1) on average (Constant time) because it uses a Hash Table. O(n) in worst case (Hash collisions, though rare).

docs.title: 52. How does a Hash Table work?
docs.text:
It uses a hash function to compute an index into an array of buckets or slots, from which the desired value can be found.

Diagram: Hash Table 

graph LR
    Key["Key: 'Apple'"] --> HashFunc[Hash Function]
    HashFunc --> Index["Index: 3"]
    Index --> Bucket[Bucket 3: Value]

docs.title: 53. What is the difference between append() and extend()?
docs.text:
• append(x): Adds x as a single element to the end of the list.
  • extend(iterable): Appends all items from the iterable to the end.
x = [1, 2]
x.append([3, 4]) # [1, 2, [3, 4]]
x.extend([3, 4]) # [1, 2, [3, 4], 3, 4]

docs.title: 54. What is collections.defaultdict?
docs.text:
A dictionary subclass that calls a factory function to supply missing values, avoiding KeyError.

from collections import defaultdict
d = defaultdict(int)
d['a'] += 1 # 'a' is initialized to 0, then incremented

docs.title: 55. What is collections.Counter?
docs.text:
A dict subclass for counting hashable objects.

from collections import Counter
c = Counter('gallahad')
# {'a': 3, 'l': 2, 'g': 1, 'h': 1, 'd': 1}

docs.title: 56. What is collections.namedtuple?
docs.text:
Factory function for creating tuple subclasses with named fields. Makes code more readable than accessing tuples by index.

from collections import namedtuple
Point = namedtuple('Point', ['x', 'y'])
p = Point(11, 22)
print(p.x) # 11

docs.title: 57. What is a Deque?
docs.text: collections.deque (Double-Ended Queue). Thread-safe, memory efficient appends and pops from either side of the deque with approx O(1) performance. Lists are O(n) for pop(0).

docs.title: 58. How are Lists implemented in Python?
docs.text: Dynamic Arrays. They store pointers to objects. When the array is full, it doubles in size (over-allocation) to achieve amortized O(1) appends.

docs.title: 59. How are Sets implemented?
docs.text: Hash Tables (similar to Dictionaries, but with dummy values). This is why set elements must be hashable.

docs.title: 60. What is heapq?
docs.text: The heapq module provides an implementation of the Heap queue algorithm (Priority Queue). It maintains the smallest element at index 0 (Min Heap).

docs.title: 61. How to merge two dictionaries?
docs.text:
Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Old method. z = x.copy(); z.update(y)
  • Path B: Python 3.5+. z = {**x, **y}
  • Path C: Python 3.9+. z = x | y (Union operator).

docs.title: 62. How to remove duplicates from a list while preserving order?
docs.text:
list(set(l)) destroys order. Solution: 

seen = set()
result = [x for x in l if not (x in seen or seen.add(x))]
(Note: seen.add(x) returns None, which is Falsy).

docs.title: 63. What is frozenset?
docs.text: An immutable version of a Python set. Because it is immutable, it is hashable and can be used as a dictionary key or an element of another set.

docs.title: 64. What is a Weak Reference?
docs.text: weakref module allows the programmer to create references to objects that do not increase the reference count. Useful for caching/caches to avoid memory leaks (holding objects in cache preventing GC).

docs.title: 65. Difference between sort() and sorted()?
docs.text:
• list.sort(): Sorts the list in-place. Returns None.
  • sorted(iterable): Returns a new sorted list. Original is unchanged.

docs.title: 66. How do you create a Class?
docs.text:
class Dog:
    species = "Canis familiaris" # Class Attribute

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name # Instance Attribute

    def bark(self):
        return f"{self.name} says Woof!"

docs.title: 67. Explain Inheritance.
docs.text:
Allows a class (Child) to derive attributes and methods from another class (Parent).

class Puppy(Dog):
    def bark(self):
        return "Yap!"

docs.title: 68. What is super()?
docs.text:
A built-in function that returns a proxy object (temporary object of the superclass) that allows you to access methods of the base class.

class Puppy(Dog):
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        super().__init__(name)
        self.age = age

docs.title: 69. Multiple Inheritance in Python?
docs.text:
Yes, Python supports it. class C(A, B): pass

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate mentions Diamond Problem.
    • Follow-up: "How does Python resolve method resolution order in the Diamond Problem?"
    • Answer: It uses the C3 Linearization algorithm (MRO).

docs.title: 70. What is MRO (Method Resolution Order)?
docs.text: The order in which Python looks for a method in a hierarchy of classes. Viewable via ClassName.__mro__ or ClassName.mro().

docs.title: 71. What are Magic Methods (Dunder Methods)?
docs.text: Special methods surrounded by double underscores. They allow instances of your classes to interact with built-in operators and functions. * __init__: Constructor. * __str__: Readable string representation (for users). * __repr__: Unambiguous string representation (for devs). * __len__: for len(). * __add__: for +.

docs.title: 72. Difference between __str__ and __repr__?
docs.text:
• __str__: Called by str(object) and print. Intended to be readable.
  • __repr__: Called by repr(object). Intended to be unambiguous. Ideally eval(repr(obj)) == obj.

docs.title: 73. What are Class Methods and Static Methods?
docs.text:
• @classmethod: Takes cls as first argument. Can access class state. Factory methods.
  • @staticmethod: No implicit first argument. Just a function inside a class namespace.
class MyClass:
    @classmethod
    def from_string(cls, s):
        return cls(...)

    @staticmethod
    def is_valid(x):
        return x > 0

docs.title: 74. What is Encapsulation?
docs.text: Restricting access to methods and variables. In Python, we use _single_leading_underscore (convention: protected) and __double_leading_underscore (name mangling: private).

docs.title: 75. What is Name Mangling?
docs.text: When using __var inside a class, Python changes the name to _ClassName__var to prevent subclasses from accidentally overriding it.

docs.title: 76. What is Polymorphism?
docs.text: The ability to present the same interface for different underlying forms (data types). Example: len() works on strings, lists, and dicts. + adds numbers but concatenates strings.

docs.title: 77. What is an Abstract Base Class (ABC)?
docs.text:
A class that cannot be instantiated and requires subclasses to implement specific methods. Used to define interfaces.

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Shape(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def area(self):
        pass

docs.title: 78. What is __slots__?
docs.text:
A mechanism to optimize memory usage by telling Python not to use a __dict__ for instances, but instead allocate space for a fixed set of attributes.

class Point:
    __slots__ = ['x', 'y']

docs.title: 79. What is Duck Typing?
docs.text: "If it looks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck." Python doesn't check types; it checks for the presence of methods/attributes at runtime.

docs.title: 80. What is a Metaclass?
docs.text: A class of a class. A class defines how an instance behaves; a metaclass defines how a class behaves. Everything in Python is an object, including classes. The default metaclass is type. Used for: Frameworks, API registration, singleton patterns.

docs.title: 81. What is a Decorator?
docs.text:
A design pattern that allows a user to add new functionality to an existing object without modifying its structure. In Python, it is a function that takes another function as an argument.

def my_decorator(func):
    def wrapper():
        print("Before")
        func()
        print("After")
    return wrapper

@my_decorator
def say_hello():
    print("Hello!")

docs.title: 82. How do you create a decorator with arguments?
docs.text:
You need three levels of nested functions.

def repeat(num_times):
    def decorator_repeat(func):
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            for _ in range(num_times):
                func(*args, **kwargs)
        return wrapper
    return decorator_repeat

@repeat(3)
def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello {name}")

docs.title: 83. What is functools.wraps?
docs.text: A decorator used when defining a decorator. It copies the metadata (name, docstring) of the original function to the wrapper function. Without it, debugging is hard (function name becomes wrapper).

docs.title: 84. What is a Generator?
docs.text: A function that returns an iterator. It looks like a normal function except that it contains yield expressions. It generates a series of values over time, pausing execution and saving state between each yield.

docs.title: 85. Generator vs Iterator?
docs.text:
• Every generator is an iterator, but not vice versa.
  • Generators are easier to write (auto __iter__ and __next__).

docs.title: 86. What is a Context Manager?
docs.text:
An object that defines the runtime context to be established when executing a with statement. Must implement __enter__ and __exit__.

class FileManager:
    def __init__(self, name, mode):
        self.file = open(name, mode)
    def __enter__(self):
        return self.file
    def __exit__(self, type, value, traceback):
        self.file.close()

docs.title: 87. What is the contextlib module?
docs.text: Utilities for creating context managers. @contextlib.contextmanager decorator allows creating a context manager using a generator function (yield separates enter and exit logic).

docs.title: 88. Explain async and await (Asyncio).
docs.text:
• async def: Defines a coroutine.
  • await: Pauses execution of the coroutine until the awaitable (IO operation) completes. Used for concurrency (single-threaded cooperative multitasking), best for IO-bound tasks.

docs.title: 89. Threading vs Multiprocessing?
docs.text: Feature Threading Multiprocessing Memory Shared Separate GIL Yes (limits CPU parallelism) No (Bypasses GIL) Use Case I/O Bound (Network, Disk) CPU Bound (Calculations) Overhead Low High (Process creation)

docs.title: 90. What is a descriptor?
docs.text: An object attribute with "binding behavior", one whose attribute access has been overridden by methods in the descriptor protocol: __get__, __set__, and __delete__. Underlies properties, methods, static methods, class methods, and super().

docs.title: 91. What is the property decorator?
docs.text:
A built-in descriptor that turns a method into a read-only attribute (getter), and allows defining setters and deleters.

class C:
    def __init__(self):
        self._x = None
    @property
    def x(self):
        return self._x
    @x.setter
    def x(self, value):
        self._x = value

docs.title: 92. How does Python handle circular imports?
docs.text: If module A imports B, and B imports A, it can cause an ImportError. Solutions: 1. Import inside the function/method (defer import). 2. Restructure code to remove circular dependency.

docs.title: 93. What is the __call__ method?
docs.text:
Allows an instance of a class to be called as a function.

class Adder:
    def __call__(self, x, y):
        return x + y

add = Adder()
print(add(2, 3)) # 5

docs.title: 94. What is Pickling and Unpickling?
docs.text:
• Pickling: Serializing a Python object structure into a byte stream.
  • Unpickling: Deserializing the byte stream back into an object.
  • Security Risk: Never unpickle data received from an untrusted source (can execute arbitrary code).

docs.title: 95. What is the difference between __new__ and __init__?
docs.text:
• __new__: Static method. Creates the instance. Returns the instance.
  • __init__: Instance method. Initializes the instance. Returns None. Use __new__ when subclassing immutable types like tuple or str.

docs.title: 96. What is Monkey Patching?
docs.text: Dynamically changing a piece of code (class or module) at runtime. Useful for testing (mocking), but dangerous in production code.

docs.title: 97. What is the purpose of __future__ module?
docs.text: To allow using features from future Python versions in the current version. e.g., from __future__ import print_function in Python 2.

docs.title: 98. How do you profile Python code?
docs.text:
• cProfile: Deterministic profiling of Python programs.
  • timeit: Measure execution time of small code snippets.

docs.title: 99. What are Type Hints?
docs.text:
Introduced in Python 3.5 (PEP 484). Syntax to declare the type of a variable/parameter. Python runtime ignores them, but static analysis tools (mypy) use them.

def greeting(name: str) -> str:
    return 'Hello ' + name

docs.title: 100. What is the Walrus Operator :=?
docs.text:
Introduced in Python 3.8. Assignment expressions. Allows you to assign a value to a variable as part of an expression.

if (n := len(a)) > 10:
    print(f"List is too long ({n} elements)")

End of Interview Questions

docs.title: Study Guide
docs.text:
To deepen your understanding of these concepts, check out the following resources:

  • Official Documentation: Python Docs
  • Internal Style Guide: Python Style Guide

docs.title: Software Engineering Interview Questions & Answers (100+)
docs.text:
What's on this page

  • Core content for this topic in the Inkorporated enterprise OS.
  • Practical guidance, roles, or standards as applicable.

What this enables

  • Consistent enterprise operations and decision-making.
  • Shared language for humans and cyborg AI agents.

This guide contains 100+ Software Engineering interview questions, covering Algorithms, System Design, OS, Networking, and Soft Skills. Each question includes a model answer and potential follow-up paths.

docs.title: 1. Explain Big O Notation.
docs.text:
Big O notation describes the worst-case performance or complexity of an algorithm. It characterizes the execution time or space used as the input size ($n$) grows.

Notation Name Example Algorithm $O(1)$ Constant Accessing array index $O(\log n)$ Logarithmic Binary Search $O(n)$ Linear Linear Search $O(n \log n)$ Linearithmic Merge Sort $O(n^2)$ Quadratic Bubble Sort

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate mentions Space Complexity.
    • Follow-up: "What is the space complexity of a recursive Fibonacci function without memoization?"
    • Answer: $O(n)$ (stack depth).

docs.title: 2. Array vs. Linked List?
docs.text:
• Array: Contiguous memory. $O(1)$ access. $O(n)$ insertion/deletion (shifting). Fixed size (usually).
  • Linked List: Non-contiguous. $O(n)$ access. $O(1)$ insertion/deletion (if pointer known). Dynamic size.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Cache Locality.
    • Follow-up: "Why are Arrays generally faster for iteration than Linked Lists?"
    • Answer: Spatial locality / CPU caching. Arrays are contiguous blocks.

docs.title: 3. What is a Hash Table?
docs.text:
A data structure that implements an associative array abstract data type, a structure that can map keys to values. It uses a hash function to compute an index into an array of buckets or slots.

graph LR
    Key --> HashFunction
    HashFunction --> Index
    Index --> Bucket[Bucket / Storage]

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Collisions.
    • Follow-up: "How do you handle collisions?"
    • Answer: Chaining (Linked Lists in buckets) or Open Addressing (Probing).

docs.title: 4. Stack vs. Queue?
docs.text:
• Stack: LIFO (Last In, First Out). Operations: push, pop. Used in recursion, undo mechanisms.
  • Queue: FIFO (First In, First Out). Operations: enqueue, dequeue. Used in job scheduling, BFS.

docs.title: 5. Explain Binary Search.
docs.text:
An efficient algorithm for finding an item from a sorted list of items. It works by repeatedly dividing in half the portion of the list that could contain the item.

Time Complexity: $O(\log n)$

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Pre-requisites.
    • Follow-up: "What happens if the array is not sorted?"
    • Answer: Binary search fails. You must sort first ($O(n \log n)$) or use Linear Search ($O(n)$).

docs.title: 6. What is a Binary Search Tree (BST)?
docs.text:
A node-based binary tree data structure which has the following properties: * The left subtree of a node contains only nodes with keys lesser than the node’s key. * The right subtree of a node contains only nodes with keys greater than the node’s key.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Balancing.
    • Follow-up: "What is the worst-case search time in a BST?"
    • Answer: $O(n)$ if the tree becomes a skewed line. Balanced trees (AVL, Red-Black) guarantee $O(\log n)$.

docs.title: 7. BFS vs. DFS?
docs.text:
• BFS (Breadth-First Search): Explores neighbor nodes first. Uses a Queue. Good for finding shortest path in unweighted graphs.
  • DFS (Depth-First Search): Explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking. Uses a Stack (recursion). Good for puzzles, topological sort.

docs.title: 8. Explain QuickSort.
docs.text:
A divide-and-conquer algorithm. It picks an element as a pivot and partitions the given array around the picked pivot.

  • Best/Avg: $O(n \log n)$
  • Worst: $O(n^2)$ (if pivot is always smallest/largest)

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Pivot Selection.
    • Follow-up: "How can you avoid the worst-case scenario?"
    • Answer: Pick a random pivot or median-of-three.

docs.title: 9. Explain Merge Sort.
docs.text:
A divide-and-conquer algorithm that divides the input array into two halves, calls itself for the two halves, and then merges the two sorted halves.

  • Complexity: Always $O(n \log n)$.
  • Stability: Stable sort (maintains relative order of equal elements).

docs.title: 10. What is Dynamic Programming?
docs.text:
A method for solving complex problems by breaking them down into simpler subproblems. It is applicable to problems exhibiting overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure.

Two approaches: 1. Memoization (Top-Down): Cache results of recursive calls. 2. Tabulation (Bottom-Up): Fill a table iteratively.

docs.title: 11. What is a Priority Queue?
docs.text: A generic data structure where each element has a "priority" associated with it. Elements with high priority are served before elements with low priority. Usually implemented with a Heap.

docs.title: 12. Min-Heap vs. Max-Heap?
docs.text:
• Min-Heap: The key at the root must be minimum among all keys present in the Binary Heap. This property must be recursively true for all nodes.
  • Max-Heap: The key at the root must be maximum.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Complexity.
    • Follow-up: "Time complexity to insert or extract min/max?"
    • Answer: $O(\log n)$ to maintain the heap property.

docs.title: 13. What is Recursion?
docs.text: A process where a function calls itself as a subroutine. Must have: 1. Base Case: To stop the recursion. 2. Recursive Step: To move closer to the base case.

docs.title: 14. Invert a Binary Tree.
docs.text:
Swap the left and right children of every node.

def invertTree(root):
    if not root: return None
    root.left, root.right = invertTree(root.right), invertTree(root.left)
    return root

docs.title: 15. Detect a cycle in a Linked List.
docs.text: Floyd’s Cycle-Finding Algorithm (Tortoise and Hare): Use two pointers. One moves 1 step, the other moves 2 steps. If they meet, there is a cycle.

docs.title: 16. What is the difference between a Graph and a Tree?
docs.text: A Tree is a special kind of Graph that is: 1. Connected. 2. Acyclic (No cycles). 3. Has $N$ nodes and $N-1$ edges.

docs.title: 17. Explain 'Greedy' Algorithms.
docs.text: An algorithmic paradigm that follows the problem-solving heuristic of making the locally optimal choice at each stage with the hope of finding a global optimum. Example: Dijkstra's Algorithm, Huffman Coding.

docs.title: 18. How to find duplicates in an array in $O(n)$ time?
docs.text: Use a HashSet or a Frequency Map. Iterate through the array; if the element is already in the set, it's a duplicate.

docs.title: 19. What is a Trie (Prefix Tree)?
docs.text: A tree-like data structure used to store a dynamic set of strings where the keys are usually strings. Use Case: Autocomplete systems.

docs.title: 20. String Immutability.
docs.text: In many languages (Java, Python, C#), strings are immutable. You cannot change characters in place; you create a new string. Reason: Security, Thread-safety, String Pool optimization.

docs.title: 21. Vertical vs. Horizontal Scaling?
docs.text: Feature Vertical (Scale Up) Horizontal (Scale Out) Definition Add more power (CPU, RAM) to existing machine. Add more machines to the pool. Downtime Usually requires downtime to upgrade. No downtime (add nodes dynamically). Limit Hard hardware limits. Infinite (theoretical). Cost Exponentially expensive for high-end hardware. Linear cost (commodity hardware).

docs.title: 22. What is a Load Balancer?
docs.text: A device that acts as a reverse proxy and distributes network or application traffic across a number of servers. * Layer 4 (Transport): Based on IP/Port. * Layer 7 (Application): Based on URL, Cookies, Headers.

docs.title: 23. Explain CAP Theorem.
docs.text:
In a distributed data store, you can only guarantee 2 out of 3: 1. Consistency: Every read receives the most recent write or an error. 2. Availability: Every request receives a (non-error) response, without the guarantee that it contains the most recent write. 3. Partition Tolerance: The system continues to operate despite an arbitrary number of messages being dropped or delayed by the network.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Real world.
    • Follow-up: "Can you sacrifice P?"
    • Answer: No, network partitions are inevitable. You must choose between CP (Mongo, Redis) and AP (Cassandra, Dynamo).

docs.title: 24. Monolithic vs. Microservices Architecture?
docs.text:
• Monolith: Single codebase, single build, single deployment. Simple to start, hard to scale teams.
  • Microservices: Collection of loosely coupled services. Independent deployment, scalable, complex to manage (network latency, consistency).

docs.title: 25. What is Database Sharding?
docs.text: A type of database partitioning that separates very large databases the into smaller, faster, more easily managed parts called data shards. * Key: Shard Key selection is critical to avoid "hot shards".

docs.title: 26. What is Caching?
docs.text: Storing copies of data in a temporary storage location (cache) so that future requests for that data can be served faster. * Types: Browser, CDN, API Gateway, Application (Memcached/Redis), Database.

docs.title: 27. Cache Eviction Policies?
docs.text:
• LRU (Least Recently Used): Discard items not used for the longest time.
  • LFU (Least Frequently Used): Discard items used least often.
  • FIFO (First In, First Out).

docs.title: 28. What is a CDN (Content Delivery Network)?
docs.text: A geographically distributed group of servers which work together to provide fast delivery of Internet content. It caches static assets (images, CSS, JS) closer to the user.

docs.title: 29. SQL vs. NoSQL?
docs.text:
• SQL (Relational): Structured, Schema-based, ACID, Vertical Scaling. (MySQL, Postgres).
  • NoSQL (Non-Relational): Unstructured/Semi-structured, Schema-less, BASE, Horizontal Scaling. (MongoDB, Cassandra).

docs.title: 30. What is Consistent Hashing?
docs.text: A distributed hashing scheme that operates independently of the number of servers or objects in a distributed hash table. It minimizes reorganization of keys when a server is added or removed.

docs.title: 31. What is a Reverse Proxy?
docs.text: A server that sits in front of web servers and forwards client (e.g. browser) requests to those web servers. Benefits: Load Balancing, Security, Caching, SSL Termination.

docs.title: 32. Rate Limiting algorithms.
docs.text:
• Token Bucket: Tokens are added at a fixed rate. Request consumes a token.
  • Leaky Bucket: Requests enter a queue and are processed at a constant rate.
  • Fixed Window: Count requests per minute.
  • Sliding Window: More smooth than fixed window.

docs.title: 33. What is a Message Queue?
docs.text: A form of asynchronous service-to-service communication used in serverless and microservices architectures. (RabbitMQ, Kafka, SQS). Benefit: Decoupling, Buffering, Reliability.

docs.title: 34. Throughput vs. Latency?
docs.text:
• Latency: Time taken to process a single request (Speed).
  • Throughput: Number of requests processed per second (Capacity).

docs.title: 35. Explain "Backpressure".
docs.text: When a system is overwhelmed by data/requests, it pushes back against the producer to slow down, preventing the system from crashing.

docs.title: 36. Polling vs. WebSockets vs. Server-Sent Events (SSE)?
docs.text:
• Polling: Client asks server "New data?" periodically. (Inefficient).
  • Long Polling: Client asks, server holds connection open until data is available.
  • WebSockets: Full-duplex (two-way) communication over single TCP connection.
  • SSE: One-way (Server to Client) streaming.

docs.title: 37. What is Database Replication?
docs.text: Copying data from one database server (primary) to others (replicas). * Master-Slave: Write to Master, Read from Slaves. * Master-Master: Write to any node (Complex conflict resolution).

docs.title: 38. Single Point of Failure (SPOF).
docs.text: A part of a system that, if it fails, will stop the entire system from working. Solution: Redundancy (Backup servers, Clusters).

docs.title: 39. Idempotency.
docs.text: An operation is idempotent if applying it multiple times has the same effect as applying it once. * GET/PUT/DELETE are idempotent. * POST is generally not.

docs.title: 40. Design a URL Shortener (TinyURL).
docs.text: Key Components: 1. API: create(long_url) -> short_url, get(short_url) -> long_url (redirect). 2. Algorithm: Base62 encoding of a unique ID. 3. Storage: Key-Value store (fast lookups).

docs.title: 41. Process vs. Thread?
docs.text: Feature Process Thread Definition An instance of a program in execution. A sequence of instructions within a process. Memory Isolated memory space. Shared memory (Heap) within process. Overhead High (Context switch is slow). Low (Lightweight context switch). Communication IPC (Pipes, Sockets). Direct memory access.

docs.title: 42. What is Concurrency vs. Parallelism?
docs.text:
• Concurrency: Handling multiple tasks at once (interleaving execution). Structure of the program.
  • Parallelism: Doing multiple tasks at once (simultaneous execution). Hardware execution.

docs.title: 43. What is a Deadlock?
docs.text:
A situation where a set of processes are blocked because each process is holding a resource and waiting for another resource acquired by some other process.

Necessary Conditions (Coffman Conditions): 1. Mutual Exclusion. 2. Hold and Wait. 3. No Preemption. 4. Circular Wait.

docs.title: 44. What is a Semaphore?
docs.text: A variable or abstract data type used to control access to a common resource by multiple processes in a concurrent system such as a multitasking operating system. * Binary Semaphore (Mutex): 0 or 1. * Counting Semaphore: Allow $N$ accessors.

docs.title: 45. Explain Virtual Memory.
docs.text:
A memory management technique that provides an "idealized abstraction" of the storage resources that are actually available on a given machine. It maps memory addresses used by a program, called virtual addresses, into physical addresses in computer memory.

Benefit: Process isolation, ability to use more memory than physically available (Paging/Swapping).

docs.title: 46. Stack vs. Heap Memory?
docs.text:
• Stack: Static memory allocation. Stores local variables, function calls. Fast access. Automatic deallocation when function returns.
  • Heap: Dynamic memory allocation. Stores objects. Slower access. Manual (C++) or Garbage Collected (Java/Python) deallocation.

docs.title: 47. What is a Context Switch?
docs.text: The process of storing the state of a process or thread, so that it can be restored and resume execution later. This allows multiple processes to share a single CPU. It is computationally expensive.

docs.title: 48. What is a Race Condition?
docs.text: A condition where the system's substantive behavior is dependent on the sequence or timing of other uncontrollable events. Occurs when two threads access shared data and try to change it at the same time.

docs.title: 49. Static vs. Dynamic Linking?
docs.text:
• Static: Libraries are copied into the executable at compile time. Larger binary, no dependency issues.
  • Dynamic: Libraries are loaded at runtime. Smaller binary, shared memory efficiency, "DLL Hell" potential.

docs.title: 50. What is a System Call?
docs.text: The programmatic way in which a computer program requests a service from the kernel of the operating system (e.g., File I/O, process creation).

docs.title: 51. Compiler vs. Interpreter?
docs.text:
• Compiler: Translates entire source code into machine code before execution. (C++, Go). Faster execution.
  • Interpreter: Translates source code line-by-line during execution. (Python, Ruby). Faster development cycle.

docs.title: 52. What is Garbage Collection?
docs.text:
A form of automatic memory management. The garbage collector attempts to reclaim memory which was allocated by the program, but is no longer referenced.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: How it works.
    • Follow-up: "What is 'Stop the World'?"
    • Answer: A pause in application execution while the GC runs.

docs.title: 53. Big Endian vs. Little Endian?
docs.text: Order of bytes. * Big Endian: Most significant byte first (at lowest address). (Networking protocols). * Little Endian: Least significant byte first. (x86 architecture).

docs.title: 54. What is Thrashing?
docs.text: When the computer's virtual memory subsystem is in a constant state of paging (swapping data between RAM and Disk), rapidly exchanging data for data on disk, to the exclusion of most application-level processing.

docs.title: 55. What is an Inode?
docs.text: A data structure in a Unix-style file system that describes a file-system object like a file or a directory. It stores attributes (permissions, owner, size) and disk block locations, but not the filename.

docs.title: 56. What happens when you type a URL in the browser?
docs.text:
1. DNS Lookup (Domain -> IP).
  2. TCP Handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK).
  3. SSL/TLS Handshake (if HTTPS).
  4. HTTP GET Request.
  5. Server processes and sends HTTP Response.
  6. Browser renders content.

docs.title: 57. TCP vs. UDP?
docs.text:
• TCP (Transmission Control Protocol): Connection-oriented, reliable, ordered, flow control. (Web, Email).
  • UDP (User Datagram Protocol): Connectionless, unreliable, no ordering, fast. (Streaming, Gaming).

docs.title: 58. Explain the OSI Model.
docs.text:
1. Physical (Cables)
  2. Data Link (MAC, Switches)
  3. Network (IP, Routers)
  4. Transport (TCP/UDP)
  5. Session
  6. Presentation (Encryption)
  7. Application (HTTP, FTP)

docs.title: 59. What is a Zombie Process?
docs.text: A process that has completed execution but still has an entry in the process table. This occurs for child processes that have stayed alive but their parent has not yet waited for them (called wait()).

docs.title: 60. Hard Link vs. Soft Link?
docs.text:
• Hard Link: Direct pointer to the inode. Deleting original file doesn't affect hard link. Cannot cross file systems.
  • Soft (Symbolic) Link: Pointer to the file name/path. If original is deleted, link is broken. Can cross file systems.

docs.title: 61. HTTP Methods.
docs.text:
• GET: Retrieve data.
  • POST: Submit data (create).
  • PUT: Update data (replace entirely).
  • PATCH: Partial update.
  • DELETE: Remove data.

docs.title: 62. HTTP Status Codes.
docs.text:
• 2xx: Success (200 OK, 201 Created).
  • 3xx: Redirection (301 Moved Permanently, 304 Not Modified).
  • 4xx: Client Error (400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found).
  • 5xx: Server Error (500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway).

docs.title: 63. HTTPS vs. HTTP.
docs.text: HTTPS is HTTP over SSL/TLS. It encrypts communication using Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) to ensure confidentiality, integrity, and authentication.

docs.title: 64. REST vs. GraphQL?
docs.text:
• REST: Resource-based. Multiple endpoints (/users, /posts). Over-fetching/Under-fetching common.
  • GraphQL: Query language. Single endpoint. Client asks for exactly what it needs.

docs.title: 65. What is a Cookie?
docs.text: Small piece of data sent from a website and stored on the user's computer by the user's web browser while the user is browsing. Used for Session management, Personalization, Tracking.

docs.title: 66. Session vs. Token (JWT) Authentication?
docs.text:
• Session: Server stores session data in memory/DB. Client sends SessionID cookie. Stateful.
  • Token (JWT): Server signs a token with data. Client stores token. Server validates signature. Stateless.

docs.title: 67. What is CORS?
docs.text: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing. A security feature where a browser blocks a web page from making requests to a different domain than the one that served the web page, unless the server explicitly allows it (via Headers like Access-Control-Allow-Origin).

docs.title: 68. LocalStorage vs. SessionStorage vs. Cookies?
docs.text: Feature Cookie LocalStorage SessionStorage Capacity 4KB 5-10MB 5-10MB Expiry Manual Never On Tab Close Sent to Server Yes (Every Request) No No

docs.title: 69. What is DNS?
docs.text: Domain Name System. The phonebook of the internet. Translates human-readable domain names (google.com) to IP addresses (142.250.190.46).

docs.title: 70. What is SQL Injection?
docs.text: A code injection technique where an attacker executes malicious SQL statements that control a web application's database server. Prevention: Prepared Statements (Parameterized Queries).

docs.title: 71. What is XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)?
docs.text: A vulnerability where an attacker injects malicious scripts into content from otherwise trusted websites. Prevention: Content Security Policy (CSP), Escaping/Sanitizing inputs.

docs.title: 72. What is CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)?
docs.text: An attack that forces an end user to execute unwanted actions on a web application in which they're currently authenticated. Prevention: Anti-CSRF Tokens.

docs.title: 73. What is a Webhook?
docs.text: A way for an app to provide other applications with real-time information. A "user-defined HTTP callback".

docs.title: 74. TCP 3-Way Handshake.
docs.text:
1. SYN: Client sends SYN to Server ("I want to connect").
  2. SYN-ACK: Server replies with SYN-ACK ("I acknowledge, let's connect").
  3. ACK: Client sends ACK ("Connection established").

docs.title: 75. Explain 'Keep-Alive'.
docs.text: An instruction that allows a single TCP connection to remain open for multiple HTTP requests/responses, reducing latency (avoiding repeated handshakes).

docs.title: 76. Forward Proxy vs. Reverse Proxy?
docs.text:
• Forward: Sits before the client. Hides client identity. (e.g., VPN, bypassing firewalls).
  • Reverse: Sits before the server. Hides server identity. (e.g., Load Balancer).

docs.title: 77. What is a Subnet Mask?
docs.text: A 32-bit number that masks an IP address, and divides the IP address into network address and host address.

docs.title: 78. What is 'localhost' and 127.0.0.1?
docs.text: The loopback address. It points back to the computer you are currently using.

docs.title: 79. What is dependency injection?
docs.text: A design pattern in which a class requests dependencies from external sources rather than creating them. Benefit: Decoupling, easier testing (mocking).

docs.title: 80. Explain 'Stateless' protocol.
docs.text: A protocol where each request is treated as an independent transaction that is unrelated to any previous request. HTTP is stateless.

docs.title: 81. Explain CI/CD.
docs.text:
• CI (Continuous Integration): Developers merge their changes back to the main branch as often as possible. Automated builds and tests run.
  • CD (Continuous Delivery/Deployment): Automatically releasing code changes to a repository or production.

docs.title: 82. What is Git?
docs.text:
A distributed version control system for tracking changes in source code during software development.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Git vs SVN.
    • Follow-up: "What does 'distributed' mean?"
    • Answer: Every developer has a full copy of the repository history.

docs.title: 83. Merge vs. Rebase?
docs.text:
• Merge: Creates a new commit, preserves history structure. Non-destructive.
  • Rebase: Moves the entire feature branch to begin on the tip of the master branch. Cleaner history (linear), but destructive (rewrites history).

docs.title: 84. What is Agile?
docs.text: A project management methodology characterized by the division of tasks into short phases of work and frequent reassessment and adaptation of plans.

docs.title: 85. Scrum vs. Kanban?
docs.text:
• Scrum: Fixed sprints (e.g., 2 weeks). Roles (Scrum Master, PO). Ceremonies.
  • Kanban: Continuous flow. Visualize work. Limit WIP (Work In Progress). No fixed sprints.

docs.title: 86. What is TDD (Test Driven Development)?
docs.text: Process: 1. Write a failing test. 2. Write just enough code to pass the test. 3. Refactor.

docs.title: 87. Docker vs. Virtual Machine?
docs.text:
• VM: Virtualizes hardware. Heavy. Includes full OS.
  • Docker (Container): Virtualizes OS. Lightweight. Shares Host OS kernel.

docs.title: 88. What is Kubernetes (K8s)?
docs.text: An open-source system for automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications (Orchestration).

docs.title: 89. Explain SOLID principles.
docs.text:
• S: Single Responsibility Principle.
  • O: Open/Closed Principle.
  • L: Liskov Substitution Principle.
  • I: Interface Segregation Principle.
  • D: Dependency Inversion Principle.

docs.title: 90. What is Technical Debt?
docs.text: The implied cost of additional rework caused by choosing an easy (limited) solution now instead of using a better approach that would take longer.

docs.title: 91. How do you handle a disagreement with a team member?
docs.text: STAR Method: * S/T: Situation/Task (Disagreement on API design). * A: Action (Listened, understood their view, proposed compromise or data-driven decision). * R: Result (Reached consensus, improved relationship).

docs.title: 92. Describe a challenging bug you fixed.
docs.text: Look for: Process of debugging. Logging, reproducing, isolating, fixing, adding regression test.

docs.title: 93. What is Code Review?
docs.text: A systematic examination of computer source code. Goals: Find bugs, improve quality, knowledge sharing, consistency.

docs.title: 94. What is "Blue/Green Deployment"?
docs.text: A technique that reduces downtime and risk by running two identical production environments called Blue and Green. At any time, one is live (Blue). You deploy to Green. Once tested, you switch the router to Green.

docs.title: 95. What is "Canary Deployment"?
docs.text: Rolling out a new version to a small subset of users (canaries) before rolling it out to the entire infrastructure.

docs.title: 96. What is Infrastructure as Code (IaC)?
docs.text: Managing and provisioning computer data centers through machine-readable definition files, rather than physical hardware configuration or interactive configuration tools. (Terraform, CloudFormation).

docs.title: 97. Pair Programming pros/cons?
docs.text:
• Pros: Fewer bugs, knowledge sharing, focus.
  • Cons: Exhausting, personality clashes, short-term velocity drop.

docs.title: 98. How do you stay updated with technology?
docs.text: Blogs (HackerNews), Conferences, Side Projects, Reading Docs, Twitter/X.

docs.title: 99. Explain the "Bus Factor".
docs.text: The minimum number of team members that have to disappear from a project before the project stalls due to lack of knowledgeable or competent personnel. Goal: Increase Bus Factor (Knowledge Sharing).

docs.title: 100. What happens when you type ls -l in a shell?
docs.text:
1. Shell reads input.
  2. Parses tokens.
  3. Checks aliases/functions.
  4. Checks PATH for executable.
  5. fork() to create child process.
  6. exec() to run ls.
  7. ls reads directory entries and prints formatted output.
  8. Parent process wait()s for child to finish.
  9. Shell prints prompt.

End of Questions

docs.title: SQL Interview Questions & Answers (100+)
docs.text:
What's on this page

  • Core content for this topic in the Inkorporated enterprise OS.
  • Practical guidance, roles, or standards as applicable.

What this enables

  • Consistent enterprise operations and decision-making.
  • Shared language for humans and cyborg AI agents.

This guide contains 100+ SQL interview questions, ranging from basic to advanced. Each question includes a model answer and potential follow-up paths based on the candidate's response.

docs.title: 1. What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE, and DROP?
docs.text:
Command Type Description Rollback? Performance DELETE DML Removes specific rows based on a WHERE clause. Yes Slower (logs per row) TRUNCATE DDL Removes all rows from a table. Resets identity. No (usually) Faster (minimal logging) DROP DDL Removes the entire table structure and data. No Fast

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate mentions transaction logs.

    • Follow-up: "Why does TRUNCATE generate less log volume than DELETE?"
    • Answer: TRUNCATE logs the deallocation of data pages, while DELETE logs the deletion of individual rows.

  • Path B: Candidate focuses on the WHERE clause.

    • Follow-up: "Can you use TRUNCATE with a WHERE clause?"
    • Answer: No, TRUNCATE is all-or-nothing for the table data.

docs.title: 2. Explain the order of execution in a SQL query.
docs.text:
Most candidates write SQL in the order SELECT -> FROM -> WHERE. However, the engine executes them differently.

graph LR
    A[FROM/JOIN] --> B[WHERE]
    B --> C[GROUP BY]
    C --> D[HAVING]
    D --> E[SELECT]
    E --> F[ORDER BY]
    F --> G[LIMIT]

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate gets it right.

    • Follow-up: "Since SELECT is executed after WHERE, can I use a column alias defined in SELECT inside the WHERE clause?"
    • Answer: No, because the WHERE clause is evaluated before the SELECT clause generates the alias.

  • Path B: Candidate forgets HAVING.

    • Follow-up: "Where does HAVING fit in? Before or after GROUP BY?"
    • Answer: After GROUP BY, as it filters the aggregated groups.

docs.title: 3. What is a Primary Key?
docs.text:
A Primary Key is a column (or set of columns) that uniquely identifies each row in a table. It must contain UNIQUE values and cannot be NULL.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate mentions 'Composite Keys'.
    • Follow-up: "When would you use a composite primary key over a surrogate key (like an auto-incrementing ID)?"
    • Answer: When there is a natural unique combination of data (e.g., StudentId + CourseId in an enrollment table) and you want to enforce that uniqueness strictly without an extra ID column.

docs.title: 4. What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
docs.text:
• WHERE: Filters rows before aggregation.
  • HAVING: Filters groups after aggregation.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate is unsure.
    • Follow-up: "Can I use count(*) in a WHERE clause?"
    • Answer: No, aggregate functions cannot be used in WHERE. They must be used in HAVING.

docs.title: 5. What are the different types of Normalization?
docs.text:
Normalization organizes data to reduce redundancy and improve data integrity.

  • 1NF: Atomic values (no repeating groups).
  • 2NF: 1NF + No partial dependency (all non-key attributes depend on the whole primary key).
  • 3NF: 2NF + No transitive dependency (non-key attributes depend only on the primary key).

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate mentions Denormalization.
    • Follow-up: "Why would we ever want to denormalize a database?"
    • Answer: For read performance. Reducing joins by keeping redundant data can speed up complex queries (e.g., in Data Warehousing).

docs.title: 6. What is a Foreign Key?
docs.text:
A Foreign Key is a field (or collection of fields) in one table, that refers to the Primary Key in another table. It enforces Referential Integrity.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate mentions 'Cascading'.
    • Follow-up: "What does ON DELETE CASCADE do?"
    • Answer: If the parent record is deleted, all child records referencing it are automatically deleted.

docs.title: 7. What is UNION vs UNION ALL?
docs.text:
• UNION: Combines result sets of two or more SELECT statements and removes duplicates.
  • UNION ALL: Combines result sets and keeps duplicates.

Chart: Performance Comparison

Operation Sorts Data? Removes Duplicates? Speed UNION Yes Yes Slower UNION ALL No No Faster

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate focuses on performance.
    • Follow-up: "If you know your datasets have no overlapping data, which one should you use?"
    • Answer: UNION ALL, to save the cost of the duplicate check/sort.

docs.title: 8. Explain NULL values in SQL.
docs.text:
NULL represents missing or undefined data. It is not equal to 0 or an empty string "".

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Handling NULLs.
    • Follow-up: "What is the result of SELECT * FROM Table WHERE Column <> NULL?"
    • Answer: It returns nothing. Comparison with NULL always results in UNKNOWN. You must use IS NOT NULL.

docs.title: 9. What is a wildcard?
docs.text: Wildcards are special characters used with the LIKE operator to search patterns. * % - Represents zero or more characters. * _ - Represents a single character.

docs.title: 10. What is an Alias in SQL?
docs.text:
An alias is a temporary name given to a table or column for the duration of a specific query.

SELECT first_name AS Name
FROM employees AS e

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Code readability.
    • Follow-up: "Can aliases be used in the WHERE clause?"
    • Answer: No (standard SQL), because WHERE executes before SELECT where the alias is assigned.

docs.title: 11. What is the DISTINCT keyword used for?
docs.text: It is used to return only distinct (different) values.

docs.title: 12. What are SQL Constraints?
docs.text: Rules applied to data columns. * NOT NULL * UNIQUE * PRIMARY KEY * FOREIGN KEY * CHECK * DEFAULT

docs.title: 13. What is a View?
docs.text:
A virtual table based on the result-set of an SQL statement. It contains rows and columns, just like a real table.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate mentions security.
    • Follow-up: "How do Views improve security?"
    • Answer: They can restrict access to specific columns or rows without giving users access to the underlying full tables.

docs.title: 14. What is an Index?
docs.text:
A data structure that improves the speed of data retrieval operations on a database table.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate says 'makes everything faster'.
    • Follow-up: "Does an index make INSERT or UPDATE statements faster?"
    • Answer: No, it usually slows them down because the index must also be updated.

docs.title: 15. What is the difference between CHAR and VARCHAR?
docs.text:
• CHAR(n): Fixed length. Pads with spaces. Faster for fixed-length data.
  • VARCHAR(n): Variable length. Stores only characters used + length info. Space efficient.

docs.title: 16. What is the BETWEEN operator?
docs.text: Selects values within a given range. The values can be numbers, text, or dates. It is inclusive: begin and end values are included.

docs.title: 17. What is the IN operator?
docs.text: Allows you to specify multiple values in a WHERE clause. It is essentially a shorthand for multiple OR conditions.

docs.title: 18. What acts as a placeholder for a missing value?
docs.text: NULL.

docs.title: 19. How do you select all columns from a table named Users?
docs.text: SELECT * FROM Users;

docs.title: 20. How do you return the number of records that have non-null values in the Price column?
docs.text:
SELECT COUNT(Price) FROM Products;

(Note: COUNT(*) counts rows including nulls, COUNT(column) counts non-nulls).

docs.title: 21. Explain the different types of JOINs.
docs.text:
Join Type Description Diagram Representation INNER JOIN Returns records that have matching values in both tables. Intersection (A ∩ B) LEFT JOIN Returns all records from the left table, and the matched records from the right table. Left Circle (A) RIGHT JOIN Returns all records from the right table, and the matched records from the left table. Right Circle (B) FULL JOIN Returns all records when there is a match in either left or right table. Union (A ∪ B)

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate mentions Cross Join.
    • Follow-up: "What is a CROSS JOIN and when is it dangerous?"
    • Answer: Cartesian product. It matches every row of A with every row of B. Dangerous on large tables as it returns N*M rows.

docs.title: 22. What is a Self-Join?
docs.text:
A self-join is a regular join, but the table is joined with itself. It requires using table aliases to distinguish the two instances.

Example Scenario: Finding employees and their managers in a single Employees table.

docs.title: 23. What is a Cross Join?
docs.text:
Produces a Cartesian product of the two tables.

SELECT * FROM TableA CROSS JOIN TableB;

If TableA has 5 rows and TableB has 10 rows, the result has 50 rows.

docs.title: 24. How do you find records in Table A that are NOT in Table B?
docs.text:
Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Using LEFT JOIN.
    • Answer: 
      SELECT A.id FROM A
LEFT JOIN B ON A.id = B.id
WHERE B.id IS NULL;
  • Path B: Using NOT IN.
    • Follow-up: "What is the risk of using NOT IN if Table B contains NULLs?"
    • Answer: If the subquery returns ANY NULL, NOT IN will return an empty set. LEFT JOIN or NOT EXISTS is safer.

docs.title: 25. What is the difference between JOIN and UNION?
docs.text:
• JOIN: Combines columns from two tables based on a related column. (Horizontal growth)
  • UNION: Combines rows from two queries. (Vertical growth)

docs.title: 26. Can you join a table to itself without using a Self-Join syntax?
docs.text: Technically, no. A "Self-Join" isn't a unique keyword, it is a concept. You use standard INNER or LEFT join syntax but reference the same table twice with aliases.

docs.title: 27. What happens if you join two tables on a column that has NULL values?
docs.text: NULL values never match other NULL values in standard SQL (unless ANSI_NULLS is off, which is rare). So, rows with NULL in the joining column will typically be excluded from an INNER JOIN.

docs.title: 28. What is a Natural Join?
docs.text: A NATURAL JOIN automatically joins tables based on columns with the same name and data types. Risk: If a new column with a matching name is added to one table later, the query logic might silently change or break.

docs.title: 29. Write a query to find the second highest salary.
docs.text:
Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Using LIMIT/OFFSET. 
    SELECT Salary FROM Employees ORDER BY Salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;
  • Path B: Using Subquery MAX. 
    SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employees WHERE Salary < (SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employees);

docs.title: 30. How do you perform a "Running Total"?
docs.text:
Using a Window Function (best practice) or a Self-Join (legacy).

Best Practice: 

SELECT Date, Amount, SUM(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY Date) as RunningTotal
FROM Sales;

docs.title: 31. What is a "Fan-out" trap in Joins?
docs.text: When joining two tables with a 1-to-many relationship, and then joining a third table with a 1-to-many relationship, the intermediate result explodes, causing incorrect aggregate calculations (e.g., SUM counts rows multiple times).

docs.title: 32. What is a SEMI JOIN?
docs.text: Returns rows from the first table where one or more matches exist in the second table. Often implemented with EXISTS. Unlike a join, it doesn't duplicate rows from the first table if multiple matches exist in the second.

docs.title: 33. What is an ANTI JOIN?
docs.text: Returns rows from the first table where NO matches exist in the second table. Often implemented with NOT EXISTS.

docs.title: 34. Explain the difference between INNER JOIN and WHERE clause for filtering.
docs.text: Functionally similar for Inner Joins. However, for LEFT JOIN, placing a condition in the ON clause vs the WHERE clause is critical. * ON: Filters the join before it happens (preserves left rows). * WHERE: Filters the result after the join (turns a Left Join into an Inner Join if filtering on the right table).

docs.title: 35. What is a composite key join?
docs.text:
Joining on multiple columns. 

FROM TableA a
JOIN TableB b ON a.col1 = b.col1 AND a.col2 = b.col2

docs.title: 36. How to select random rows from a table?
docs.text:
Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: MySQL. ORDER BY RAND() LIMIT 1 (Slow on large tables).
  • Path B: SQL Server. ORDER BY NEWID().
  • Path C: PostgreSQL. ORDER BY RANDOM().

docs.title: 37. Difference between INTERSECT and MINUS (or EXCEPT)?
docs.text:
• INTERSECT: Returns rows common to both query results.
  • MINUS/EXCEPT: Returns rows in the first result but not the second.

docs.title: 38. How to find duplicate records in a table?
docs.text:
SELECT ColumnA, COUNT(*)
FROM Table
GROUP BY ColumnA
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

docs.title: 39. How do you delete duplicate rows but keep one?
docs.text:
Using CTE (Common Table Expressions) and ROW_NUMBER(): 

WITH CTE AS (
    SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ID ORDER BY ID) as rn
    FROM Table
)
DELETE FROM CTE WHERE rn > 1;

docs.title: 40. What is a recursive CTE?
docs.text:
A CTE that references itself. Useful for hierarchical data (e.g., Organization Charts, Bill of Materials).

graph TD
    A[Root] --> B[Child 1]
    A --> C[Child 2]
    B --> D[Grandchild 1]

docs.title: 41. What is the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(column_name)?
docs.text:
• COUNT(*): Counts all rows in the result set, including those with NULL values.
  • COUNT(column_name): Counts only rows where column_name is NOT NULL.

docs.title: 42. Can you group by a column that is not selected?
docs.text: Yes, standard SQL allows grouping by a column that is not in the SELECT list. However, you cannot select a non-aggregated column that is not in the GROUP BY list (unless using MySQL with specific settings or functional dependencies).

docs.title: 43. How does GROUP BY interact with NULL values?
docs.text: SQL considers all NULLs to be equal for grouping purposes. Therefore, all NULL values are grouped into a single bucket.

docs.title: 44. Write a query to find the department with the highest average salary.
docs.text:
SELECT DepartmentID, AVG(Salary) as AvgSalary
FROM Employees
GROUP BY DepartmentID
ORDER BY AvgSalary DESC
LIMIT 1;

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Using CTE.
    • Follow-up: "If there is a tie, how do you return both?"
    • Answer: Use RANK() or DENSE_RANK() in a CTE/Subquery and filter where rank = 1.

docs.title: 45. What is the HAVING clause?
docs.text: (Already covered briefly in #4, but deeper dive) It filters records that summarize the group. Example: SELECT Dept, SUM(Sal) FROM Emp GROUP BY Dept HAVING SUM(Sal) > 10000.

docs.title: 46. Can you use an alias in the HAVING clause?
docs.text: It depends on the SQL dialect. * MySQL: Yes. * SQL Server/Standard SQL: Generally No (because HAVING is evaluated before SELECT). You must repeat the aggregate function.

docs.title: 47. What is ROLLUP?
docs.text:
ROLLUP is an extension of the GROUP BY clause that produces sub-totals and a grand total.

SELECT Region, Country, SUM(Sales)
FROM Orders
GROUP BY ROLLUP (Region, Country);

docs.title: 48. What is CUBE?
docs.text:
CUBE generates sub-totals for all possible combinations of the grouping columns. It produces more rows than ROLLUP.

Table: ROLLUP vs CUBE

Group By (A, B) Resulting Groupings ROLLUP(A, B) (A, B), (A), () CUBE(A, B) (A, B), (A), (B), ()

docs.title: 49. What is GROUPING SETS?
docs.text: It allows you to specify exactly which groupings you want to compute, rather than all combinations (CUBE) or hierarchical ones (ROLLUP). It is more efficient if you only need specific aggregates.

docs.title: 50. How do you pivot data in SQL?
docs.text:
Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: CASE WHEN. (Universal standard) 
    SELECT
  SUM(CASE WHEN Year = 2020 THEN Revenue END) as Rev2020,
  SUM(CASE WHEN Year = 2021 THEN Revenue END) as Rev2021
FROM Sales;
  • Path B: PIVOT operator. (SQL Server / Oracle)

docs.title: 51. How do you unpivot data?
docs.text: Converting columns back into rows. * Use UNION ALL. * Use UNPIVOT operator (SQL Server/Oracle). * Use CROSS APPLY with VALUES (SQL Server).

docs.title: 52. What is the difference between WHERE and ON in a specific aggregation context?
docs.text: If filtering before aggregation, use WHERE. If filtering the joined rows before aggregation, use ON. Important: Filtering in WHERE on a LEFT JOINed table turns it into an INNER JOIN.

docs.title: 53. How to find the top 3 categories by sales?
docs.text:
SELECT Category, SUM(Sales)
FROM Orders
GROUP BY Category
ORDER BY SUM(Sales) DESC
LIMIT 3;

docs.title: 54. How to count distinct items in a group?
docs.text:
SELECT Department, COUNT(DISTINCT EmployeeID)
FROM Employees
GROUP BY Department;

docs.title: 55. What aggregate functions return a different data type than the input?
docs.text:
• COUNT() always returns an Integer (or BigInt).
  • AVG() usually returns a Float/Decimal, even if input is Integer.

docs.title: 56. Can you nest aggregate functions?
docs.text: No, you cannot do MAX(SUM(Salary)). You must use a subquery or CTE. Step 1: Calculate SUM(Salary) per group. Step 2: Calculate MAX() from that result.

docs.title: 57. What is the impact of indexing on aggregation?
docs.text: Indexes can significantly speed up MIN(), MAX(), and COUNT() operations, especially if the index covers the column being aggregated. A "Covering Index" avoids accessing the table rows entirely.

docs.title: 58. Calculate the percentage contribution of each row to the total sum.
docs.text:
Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Using Window Function. 
    SELECT Item, Amount,
       Amount * 100.0 / SUM(Amount) OVER() as Pct
FROM Sales;
  • Path B: Using Subquery. 
    SELECT Item, Amount,
       Amount * 100.0 / (SELECT SUM(Amount) FROM Sales)
FROM Sales;

docs.title: 59. How to find groups that have at least two specific items?
docs.text:
SELECT OrderID
FROM OrderDetails
WHERE ProductID IN ('A', 'B')
GROUP BY OrderID
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT ProductID) = 2;

docs.title: 60. What is string_agg or group_concat?
docs.text: It concatenates values from multiple rows into a single string per group. * MySQL: GROUP_CONCAT(col) * PostgreSQL: STRING_AGG(col, ',') * SQL Server: STRING_AGG(col, ',')

docs.title: 61. What is a Window Function?
docs.text: Window functions perform calculations across a set of table rows that are somehow related to the current row. Unlike aggregate functions, they do not cause rows to become grouped into a single output row.

docs.title: 62. Difference between RANK(), DENSE_RANK(), and ROW_NUMBER()?
docs.text:
Consider data: 10, 20, 20, 30

Value ROW_NUMBER() RANK() DENSE_RANK() 10 1 1 1 20 2 2 2 20 3 2 2 30 4 4 3
  • ROW_NUMBER: Unique sequential number.
  • RANK: Skips numbers after ties (1, 2, 2, 4).
  • DENSE_RANK: No gaps after ties (1, 2, 2, 3).

docs.title: 63. What is the PARTITION BY clause?
docs.text: It divides the result set into partitions (groups) to which the window function is applied. Example: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY Department ORDER BY Salary DESC) resets the counter for each Department.

docs.title: 64. What is LEAD and LAG?
docs.text:
• LAG(col, n): Accesses data from a previous row (n rows back).
  • LEAD(col, n): Accesses data from a following row (n rows forward).

Use Case: Calculating Year-Over-Year growth.

docs.title: 65. Calculate the difference between current and previous row's value.
docs.text:
SELECT Date, Value,
       Value - LAG(Value) OVER (ORDER BY Date) as Diff
FROM Metrics;

docs.title: 66. What is NTILE(n)?
docs.text: Distributes rows of an ordered partition into a specified number of approximately equal groups (buckets). Example: NTILE(4) divides data into Quartiles.

docs.title: 67. Explain the Frame clause (ROWS BETWEEN ...).
docs.text:
It defines the subset of rows within the partition to be considered for the calculation.

  • UNBOUNDED PRECEDING: Start at the first row of partition.
  • CURRENT ROW: Stop at current row.
  • n PRECEDING / FOLLOWING.

Example: Rolling 3-day Average 

AVG(Val) OVER (ORDER BY Date ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)

docs.title: 68. What are Common Table Expressions (CTEs)?
docs.text: A temporary result set that you can reference within a SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statement. Pros: Readability, recursion. Cons: Not indexed (usually), exists only for query duration.

docs.title: 69. CTE vs Subquery vs Temp Table?
docs.text: Feature CTE Subquery Temp Table Scope Single Query Single Query Session Recursive? Yes No No Indexed? No No Yes Performance Optimized by engine Optimized by engine Overhead to create

docs.title: 70. How to update a table based on values from another table?
docs.text:
UPDATE A
SET A.Value = B.Value
FROM TableA A
JOIN TableB B ON A.ID = B.ID;
(Syntax varies by dialect: MySQL uses JOIN in update, SQL Server uses FROM).

docs.title: 71. What is MERGE (or UPSERT)?
docs.text:
A single statement that performs UPDATE if a row exists, and INSERT if it does not.

MERGE INTO Target T
USING Source S ON T.id = S.id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET ...
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT ...;

docs.title: 72. Explain JSON handling in modern SQL.
docs.text: Most modern DBs (Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server) support JSON types. * Extract: json_col ->> 'key' (Postgres). * Query: WHERE json_col ->> 'tags' LIKE '%urgent%'.

docs.title: 73. What is a Stored Procedure?
docs.text:
A prepared SQL code that you can save, so the code can be reused over and over again. It can accept parameters.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Pros/Cons.
    • Follow-up: "Why are they considered bad for version control?"
    • Answer: Logic is hidden in the DB, harder to diff/review than application code.

docs.title: 74. Function vs Stored Procedure?
docs.text:
• Function: Must return a value. Cannot modify DB state (usually). Can be used in SELECT statements.
  • Procedure: Can return zero or n values. Can modify DB state. Cannot be used in SELECT statements.

docs.title: 75. What is a Trigger?
docs.text: A special type of stored procedure that automatically runs when an event occurs in the database server (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE). Risk: Can create invisible logic chains ("Magic") that are hard to debug.

docs.title: 76. How to find gaps in sequential IDs?
docs.text:
Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Using LEAD. 
    SELECT id + 1 as StartGap, next_id - 1 as EndGap
FROM (
    SELECT id, LEAD(id) OVER (ORDER BY id) as next_id
    FROM Table
) T
WHERE next_id - id > 1;

docs.title: 77. What is first_value() and last_value()?
docs.text: Returns the first or last value in an ordered set of values. Note: last_value default frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, so it often just returns the current row value unless you change the frame to UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.

docs.title: 78. What is the QUALIFY clause?
docs.text: (Used in Snowflake/Teradata) Filters the results of window functions, similar to how HAVING filters GROUP BY. Avoids the need for a subquery to filter by RANK().

docs.title: 79. How do you handle Time Zones in SQL?
docs.text: Always store in UTC (TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE in Postgres). Convert to local time only at the presentation layer or reporting query.

docs.title: 80. Identify overlapping date ranges.
docs.text:
SELECT *
FROM Bookings A
JOIN Bookings B ON A.Room = B.Room AND A.ID <> B.ID
WHERE A.Start < B.End AND A.End > B.Start;

docs.title: 81. Explain ACID properties.
docs.text:
• A - Atomicity: All or nothing. Transaction is a single unit.
  • C - Consistency: Database remains in a valid state before and after transaction.
  • I - Isolation: Transactions occur independently without interference.
  • D - Durability: Once committed, changes are permanent (survive power loss).

docs.title: 82. What are the Isolation Levels?
docs.text:
(Ordered from lowest isolation/highest concurrency to highest isolation/lowest concurrency)

  1. Read Uncommitted: Dirty reads allowed.
  2. Read Committed: No dirty reads. Phantom reads possible. (Default in many DBs).
  3. Repeatable Read: No non-repeatable reads. Phantom reads possible (prevented in some DBs like Postgres).
  4. Serializable: Strict sequential execution.

docs.title: 83. What is a "Dirty Read"?
docs.text: Reading uncommitted data from another transaction. If that transaction rolls back, you read invalid data.

docs.title: 84. What is a "Phantom Read"?
docs.text: A transaction executes a query returning a set of rows. Another transaction inserts a new row that matches the query. If the first transaction runs the query again, it sees the "phantom" row.

docs.title: 85. What is the N+1 problem?
docs.text: A performance issue where the application executes 1 initial query (N=1) and then executes N additional queries to fetch related data for each row. Fix: Use JOINs or batch fetching.

docs.title: 86. How does a B-Tree Index work?
docs.text:
It is a balanced tree structure that keeps data sorted and allows searches, sequential access, insertions, and deletions in logarithmic time.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Clustered vs Non-Clustered.
    • Follow-up: "How many clustered indexes can a table have?"
    • Answer: Only one, because it dictates the physical order of data storage.

docs.title: 87. What is Database Sharding?
docs.text: Horizontal partitioning of data across multiple databases/servers (shards) to spread load. Key Challenge: Cross-shard joins are expensive or impossible.

docs.title: 88. What is Partitioning?
docs.text: Splitting a large table into smaller, more manageable pieces (e.g., by Year). The DB engine can skip scanning partitions that don't match the query (Partition Pruning).

docs.title: 89. Explain "Explain Plan".
docs.text: A visualization of how the SQL engine intends to execute a query. Look for: Table Scans (bad), Index Seek/Scan (good), Sort operations (expensive).

docs.title: 90. What is a "Deadlock"?
docs.text: Two transactions are waiting for each other to give up a lock. The DB engine usually kills one to save the other.

docs.title: 91. Difference between OLTP and OLAP?
docs.text:
• OLTP (Online Transaction Processing): Fast, short transactions (INSERT, UPDATE). Normalized (3NF).
  • OLAP (Online Analytical Processing): Complex queries, historical data. Denormalized (Star Schema).

docs.title: 92. What is a Star Schema?
docs.text:
A data warehousing modeling technique with a central Fact Table (metrics) connected to multiple Dimension Tables (attributes).

graph TD
    Fact[Fact Sales]
    D1[Dim Date]
    D2[Dim Product]
    D3[Dim Customer]
    Fact --- D1
    Fact --- D2
    Fact --- D3

docs.title: 93. What is a Snowflake Schema?
docs.text: A variation of Star Schema where dimension tables are normalized (split into sub-dimensions). * Pros: Less space. * Cons: More joins.

docs.title: 94. How to optimize a slow query?
docs.text:
1. Check EXPLAIN plan.
  2. Add missing Indexes.
  3. Remove unnecessary columns (SELECT *).
  4. Check for Functions on columns in WHERE clause (sargability).
  5. Update Statistics.

docs.title: 95. What is "SARGable"?
docs.text: Search ARGument ABLE. A query is sargable if it can take advantage of an index. * Bad: WHERE YEAR(date_col) = 2023 (Function on column blocks index). * Good: WHERE date_col >= '2023-01-01' AND date_col < '2024-01-01'.

docs.title: 96. What is a Materialized View?
docs.text: A view whose result is physically stored (cached) on disk and refreshed periodically. Good for expensive aggregations.

docs.title: 97. What is optimistic vs pessimistic locking?
docs.text:
• Pessimistic: Lock the record as soon as you select it for update.
  • Optimistic: Don't lock. Check version/timestamp on update. If changed by someone else, fail.

docs.title: 98. What is Vertical Scaling vs Horizontal Scaling?
docs.text:
• Vertical: Bigger machine (more RAM/CPU). Easiest for SQL DBs.
  • Horizontal: More machines (Read Replicas, Sharding). Harder for SQL DBs.

docs.title: 99. What is CAP Theorem?
docs.text: In a distributed system, you can only pick 2: * Consistency. * Availability. * Partition Tolerance. * Traditional SQL DBs usually choose CA (single node) or CP (distributed).

docs.title: 100. Write a query to find the 3rd highest salary without using LIMIT/TOP.
docs.text:
SELECT Salary
FROM Employees e1
WHERE 2 = (
    SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT Salary)
    FROM Employees e2
    WHERE e2.Salary > e1.Salary
);

End of Interview Questions

docs.title: Study Guide
docs.text:
To deepen your understanding of these concepts, check out the following resources:

  • Official Documentation: Sql Docs
  • Internal Style Guide: Sql Style Guide

docs.title: System Design Interview Questions & Answers (100+)
docs.text:
What's on this page

  • Core content for this topic in the Inkorporated enterprise OS.
  • Practical guidance, roles, or standards as applicable.

What this enables

  • Consistent enterprise operations and decision-making.
  • Shared language for humans and cyborg AI agents.

This guide contains 100+ System Design interview questions, ranging from core concepts to complex distributed system scenarios. Each question includes a model answer and potential follow-up paths based on the candidate's response.

docs.title: 1. What is the difference between Vertical Scaling and Horizontal Scaling?
docs.text:
Feature Vertical Scaling (Scale Up) Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out) Definition Adding more power (CPU, RAM) to an existing machine. Adding more machines to the resource pool. Limit Hard limit based on hardware capacity. Theoretically infinite (constrained by software/network). Downtime Usually requires downtime to upgrade. No downtime (add nodes dynamically). Complexity Low (no distributed logic). High (requires load balancing, consistency mgmt).

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Candidate mentions Cost.
    • Follow-up: "At what point does vertical scaling become more expensive than horizontal?"
    • Answer: Specialized high-end hardware follows a non-linear price curve. Two medium servers are often cheaper than one super-server.
  • Path B: Candidate focuses on Databases.
    • Follow-up: "Why is it harder to horizontally scale a traditional SQL database?"
    • Answer: ACID compliance and JOINS are difficult to maintain across distributed nodes.

docs.title: 2. Explain Load Balancing (L4 vs L7).
docs.text:
A Load Balancer distributes incoming network traffic across a group of backend servers.

  • Layer 4 (Transport Layer): Routes traffic based on IP address and Port (TCP/UDP). It is packet-level load balancing.
  • Layer 7 (Application Layer): Routes traffic based on content (URL, Cookies, Headers). It is request-level load balancing.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Performance.
    • Follow-up: "Which is faster, L4 or L7?"
    • Answer: L4 is faster because it doesn't need to decrypt/inspect the payload.
  • Path B: Security.
    • Follow-up: "Why is L7 better for security?"
    • Answer: It can inspect traffic for SQL injection, terminate SSL, and implement smarter rate limiting.

docs.title: 3. What is the CAP Theorem?
docs.text:
In a distributed data store, you can strictly provide only two of the three guarantees:

  1. Consistency: Every read receives the most recent write or an error.
  2. Availability: Every request receives a (non-error) response, without the guarantee that it contains the most recent write.
  3. Partition Tolerance: The system continues to operate despite an arbitrary number of messages being dropped or delayed by the network.
graph TD
    C[Consistency] --- A[Availability]
    A --- P[Partition Tolerance]
    P --- C
    style C fill:#f9f,stroke:#333
    style A fill:#ff9,stroke:#333
    style P fill:#9ff,stroke:#333

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: "I choose CA".
    • Follow-up: "Can a distributed system actually be CA?"
    • Answer: No. In a distributed system, network partitions will happen. You effectively choose between CP (stop serving requests) or AP (serve stale data) when a partition occurs.

docs.title: 4. Compare ACID vs BASE models.
docs.text:
• ACID (Relational DBs): Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. Focuses on strict data integrity.
  • BASE (NoSQL DBs):
    • Basically Available: System guarantees availability.
    • Soft state: State may change over time, even without input.
    • Eventual consistency: System will become consistent over time.

docs.title: 5. What are the common Caching Strategies?
docs.text:
1. Cache Aside (Lazy Loading): App checks cache. If miss, reads DB, writes to cache.
  2. Read-Through: App asks cache. Cache fetches from DB if miss.
  3. Write-Through: App writes to cache and DB synchronously.
  4. Write-Back (Write-Behind): App writes to cache. Cache writes to DB asynchronously.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Write-Back.
    • Follow-up: "What is the major risk of Write-Back?"
    • Answer: Data loss if the cache crashes before flushing data to the persistent DB.

docs.title: 6. What is a CDN (Content Delivery Network)?
docs.text:
A network of geographically distributed servers that deliver static content (images, CSS, JS, videos) to users based on their location.

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Push vs Pull.
    • Follow-up: "How does the CDN get the content?"
    • Answer: Push: You upload to CDN. Pull: CDN fetches from Origin on first request (cache miss).

docs.title: 7. Stateless vs Stateful Architecture?
docs.text:
• Stateless: Server retains no client information between requests. Every request must contain all necessary info (e.g., JWT). Scales easily.
  • Stateful: Server remembers client data (Session ID) from previous requests. Harder to scale horizontally (requires Sticky Sessions).

docs.title: 8. Latency vs Throughput?
docs.text:
• Latency: Time taken to process a single request (Speed).
  • Throughput: Number of requests processed per unit time (Capacity).

Analogy: * Latency: How fast a car drives. * Throughput: How many cars pass a point per hour.

docs.title: 9. What are common Availability Patterns?
docs.text:
1. Fail-over:
    • Active-Passive: Heartbeat sends signal. If Active dies, Passive takes over.
    • Active-Active: Both handle traffic.
  2. Replication: Master-Slave, Master-Master.

docs.title: 10. How does DNS Resolution work?
docs.text:
1. Browser checks local cache.
  2. OS checks hosts file.
  3. Query sent to Recursive Resolver (ISP).
  4. Resolver queries Root Server (.) -> TLD Server (.com) -> Authoritative Name Server (example.com).
  5. IP returned to browser.

docs.title: 11. What is Consistent Hashing?
docs.text:
A technique to distribute data across nodes in a way that minimizes reorganization when nodes are added or removed. Instead of hash(key) % N, it maps keys and nodes to a "Ring" (0 to 2^32).

Candidate Response Paths:

  • Path A: Hotspots.
    • Follow-up: "What if one node is very powerful or gets too much data?"
    • Answer: Use "Virtual Nodes" (vnodes). Map one physical node to multiple points on the ring.

docs.title: 12. Forward Proxy vs Reverse Proxy?
docs.text:
• Forward Proxy: Sit before the Client. Masks the Client ID. (e.g., VPN, Corporate Filter).
  • Reverse Proxy: Sit before the Server. Masks the Server ID. (e.g., Nginx, Load Balancer).

docs.title: 13. Polling vs WebSockets vs Server-Sent Events (SSE).
docs.text: Feature Polling (Short/Long) WebSockets SSE Direction Client -> Server Bidirectional Server -> Client Connection New connection per request (Short) Persistent TCP Persistent HTTP Use Case Dashboards, low frequency Chat, Gaming News feeds, Stock Tickers

docs.title: 14. LSM Tree vs B-Tree (Database Indexing).
docs.text:
• B-Tree: (Used in SQL) Optimized for Reads. Data stored in sorted pages. Update in-place.
  • LSM (Log-Structured Merge): (Used in Cassandra, Kafka) Optimized for Writes. Appends to log, merges in background.

docs.title: 15. What are common Rate Limiting Algorithms?
docs.text:
1. Token Bucket: Tokens added at rate r. Request consumes token. (Allows Bursts).
  2. Leaky Bucket: Requests enter queue, processed at constant rate. (Smooths traffic).
  3. Fixed Window Counter: Counter resets every minute. (Edge case: double bursts at boundary).
  4. Sliding Window Log: Precise, stores timestamps. (High memory).
  5. Sliding Window Counter: Hybrid approach.
