  • Default Values: Use default values where appropriate (e.g., created_at DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP).
  • Migrations: All schema changes must be versioned and reversible (where possible).

docs.title: Performance and Optimization
docs.text:
• Indexing:
    • Index columns used in WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY, and GROUP BY clauses.
    • Avoid over-indexing; every index adds overhead to writes.
    • Use composite indexes for queries filtering on multiple columns (order matters: equality first, then range).
  • SARGable Queries: Write Search ARGumentable queries.
    • Avoid functions on indexed columns in the WHERE clause (e.g., WHERE YEAR(date_col) = 2023). Instead use range checks (WHERE date_col >= '2023-01-01' AND date_col < '2024-01-01').
    • Avoid leading wildcards in LIKE ('%value').
  • Set-Based Operations: Think in sets, not loops. Avoid cursors and procedural loops whenever possible.
  • Explain Plan: Always check the execution plan (EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN ANALYZE) for complex or slow-running queries.
  • Limit: Use LIMIT when you only need a sample or top-N results.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• SQL Injection: NEVER concatenate user input directly into SQL strings.
    • Use prepared statements / parameterized queries provided by your client library.
  • Least Privilege: Application users/roles should only have the permissions necessary (e.g., CONNECT, SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE).
    • Do not use the root or postgres superuser for applications.
    • Restrict access to DDL commands (CREATE, DROP, ALTER).
  • Sensitive Data: Encrypt sensitive data (PII, passwords) at rest and in transit. Hashing (e.g., bcrypt, argon2) is mandatory for passwords.

docs.title: Documentation and Comments
docs.text:
• Header Comments: For complex stored procedures or views, include a header comment explaining the purpose, author, and parameters.
  • Inline Comments: Use -- for inline comments. Explain why complex logic is used.
  • Schema Documentation: Use the database's comment feature (COMMENT ON TABLE, COMMENT ON COLUMN) to document the schema itself.
COMMENT ON TABLE users IS 'Stores registered user accounts';
COMMENT ON COLUMN users.status IS 'Current state of the user account (active, suspended, deleted)';

docs.title: Transaction Management
docs.text:
• ACID: Ensure operations that modify multiple tables are wrapped in a transaction to maintain Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability.
  • Explicit Transactions: Use BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK explicitly when logic requires it.
  • Locking: Be aware of locking behavior. keep transactions short to avoid blocking other operations.
  • Error Handling: Implement proper error handling in stored procedures or application code to rollback transactions on failure.

docs.title: Recommended Tools
docs.text:
• Linter: sqlfluff - A modular SQL linter and auto-formatter.
  • Formatter: sql-formatter or pgFormatter.
  • Migration Tools: Flyway, Liquibase, or language-specific tools like alembic (Python), golang-migrate (Go).
  • GUI Clients: DBeaver, DataGrip, or Postico for safe database exploration.

docs.title: Related Interview Questions
docs.text: • Practice Questions: Test your knowledge of Sql concepts.

docs.title: Starlark Style Guide
docs.text:
What's on this page

  • Core content for this topic in the Inkorporated enterprise OS.
  • Practical guidance, roles, or standards as applicable.

What this enables

  • Consistent enterprise operations and decision-making.
  • Shared language for humans and cyborg AI agents.

This document outlines the coding standards and best practices for Starlark development (used in Bazel, Buck2, etc.) within this project. Adhering to these guidelines ensures code consistency, readability, and maintainability.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
1. General Principles
  2. Code Layout
  3. Naming Conventions
  4. Build Files vs. Extensions
  5. Load Statements
  6. Macros and Rules
  7. Functions
  8. Data Structures
  9. Control Flow
  10. Error Handling
  11. Documentation
  12. Tooling

docs.title: General Principles
docs.text:
• Hermeticity: Starlark code should be hermetic. Outputs should depend only on inputs and configuration, not on the external environment (timestamps, network, absolute paths).
  • Determinism: Execution must be deterministic. Iteration order of dictionaries is fixed in Starlark, but be mindful of sets (which don't exist in Starlark, use depset or sorted lists).
  • Readability: Starlark is optimized for readability. It is often read by developers who are not experts in the build system. Keep logic simple.
  • Pythonic: Starlark is a dialect of Python. Follow Python best practices (PEP 8) where they apply and don't conflict with Starlark specifics.

docs.title: Code Layout
docs.text:
• Indentation: Use 4 spaces for indentation. Do not use tabs.
  • Line Length: Limit lines to 79 characters. This is the standard for .bzl and BUILD files (enforced by Buildifier).
  • Whitespace:
    • Use spaces around operators (=, +, +=, etc.).
    • No spaces around keyword argument assignments in calls (func(arg=value)), but spaces around default values in definitions (def func(arg = value):).
  • Blank Lines:
    • Use blank lines to separate rules and macro calls in BUILD files.
    • Use 2 blank lines between top-level function definitions in .bzl files.
  • Trailing Commas: Always use trailing commas in multi-line lists, dictionaries, and function calls. This reduces merge conflicts and makes reordering easier.
# Good
my_rule(
    name = "my_target",
    srcs = [
        "file1.cc",
        "file2.cc",
    ],
    deps = [
        ":lib",
    ],
)

docs.title: Naming Conventions
docs.text:
• Variables/Functions: snake_case.
  • Rules/Macros: snake_case.
  • Providers: PascalCase (e.g., MyInfo).
  • Constants: UPPER_CASE (e.g., DEFAULT_TIMEOUT).
  • Private Symbols: Prefix with _ (underscore). These are not exported from the .bzl file.
    • def _my_private_helper():
  • Filenames:
    • Build files: BUILD or BUILD.bazel.
    • Extension files: snake_case.bzl.

docs.title: Build Files vs. Extensions
docs.text:
• BUILD Files:
    • Should be declarative.
    • Avoid complex logic (loops, if statements) in BUILD files. Move logic to macros in .bzl files.
    • Variable definitions should be minimal.
  • .bzl Files:
    • Can contain logic, function definitions, rules, and macros.
    • Should be organized logically (loads, constants, providers, implementation functions, rule definitions, macros).

docs.title: Load Statements
docs.text:
• Placement: All load() statements must be at the top of the file, after the license header and docstring.
  • Sorting: Load statements should be sorted alphabetically by the label (first argument).
  • Symbols: Symbols loaded from a file should be sorted alphabetically.
  • Format:
load("@rules_cc//cc:defs.bzl", "cc_binary", "cc_library")
load("//path/to/package:defs.bzl", "my_macro")
  • Aliases: Avoid aliasing unless necessary for disambiguation. If used, follow original_name = "alias" (which is not supported directly in load, so load("...", other_name = "original_name")). Note: Starlark load syntax is load("file", local_name = "symbol_name").

docs.title: Macros and Rules
docs.text:
• Macros:
    • Should wrap one or more rules.
    • Must have a name argument.
    • Should usually pass **kwargs to the main underlying rule to forward common attributes like tags, visibility, testonly.
    • Use native.existing_rule() to check if a target already exists (be careful with performance).
  • Rules:
    • Implementation functions should be named _rule_name_impl.
    • Attributes should be defined clearly using attr.*.
    • Prefer executable = True and test = True where appropriate.
def my_macro(name, **kwargs):
    """Wraps a cc_binary with default settings.

    Args:
        name: The name of the target.
        **kwargs: Arguments forwarded to cc_binary.
    """
    cc_binary(
        name = name,
        copts = ["-Werror"],
        **kwargs
    )

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
• Arguments:
    • Use keyword arguments for readability, especially for booleans or when a function has many arguments.
    • Document arguments in docstrings.
  • Return Values: Keep return values simple. Structs or providers are preferred over complex dictionaries.

docs.title: Data Structures
docs.text:
• Lists vs Tuples:
    • Lists are mutable (unless frozen). Use them when you need to construct a collection.
    • Tuples are immutable. Use them for fixed collections.
    • Note: In BUILD files, lists are often used for srcs and deps.
  • Dictionaries:
    • Dictionary concatenation (+) matches Python semantics (last write wins).
    • Iteration order is deterministic (insertion order).
  • Depsets:
    • Use depset instead of lists for accumulating transitive data (like headers, object files) to avoid O(N^2) memory consumption.
    • Understand order semantics ("default", "postorder", "preorder", "topological").

docs.title: Control Flow
docs.text:
• Loops: for loops are allowed. while loops are not supported.
  • Recursion: Recursion is not allowed in Starlark.
  • Conditionals: if, elif, else behave as in Python.
  • List Comprehensions: Encouraged for succinct transformations.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
• fail(): Use fail("Error message") to stop execution with an error.
    • Use meaningful error messages.
    • Do not use print() for errors; it is for debugging only.
    • fail is preferable to assert style checks if specific error messaging is needed.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• Docstrings:
    • All exported rules, macros, and providers must have a docstring.
    • Use the Google docstring format (triple quotes).
    • Document arguments (Args:), return values (Returns:), and attributes.
  • Stardoc:
    • Write docstrings compatible with Stardoc to generate documentation automatically.
def my_rule_impl(ctx):
    """Implementation of my_rule."""
    pass

my_rule = rule(
    implementation = my_rule_impl,
    doc = """
    A rule that does something useful.

    Attributes:
        srcs: Source files.
    """,
    attrs = {
        "srcs": attr.label_list(allow_files = True),
    },
)

docs.title: Tooling
docs.text:
• Buildifier:
    • Use buildifier to format and lint Starlark code.
    • Run buildifier -r . to format all files recursively.
    • Use comments # buildifier: disable=rule-name to suppress specific warnings if absolutely necessary, but explain why.

docs.title: TypeScript Style Guide
docs.text:
What's on this page

  • Core content for this topic in the Inkorporated enterprise OS.
  • Practical guidance, roles, or standards as applicable.

What this enables

  • Consistent enterprise operations and decision-making.
  • Shared language for humans and cyborg AI agents.

This document outlines the coding standards and best practices for TypeScript development within this project. Adhering to these guidelines ensures code consistency, type safety, readability, and maintainability.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
1. General Principles
  2. Project Configuration
  3. Naming Conventions
  4. Types and Type Safety
  5. Variables and Constants
  6. Functions
  7. Control Flow
  8. Data Structures
  9. Classes and OOP
  10. Asynchronous Programming
  11. Modules and Imports
  12. Error Handling
  13. Comments and Documentation
  14. Testing
  15. Recommended Tools

docs.title: General Principles
docs.text:
• Consistency: Consistency with the existing codebase is paramount. If a pattern is established, follow it.
  • Type Safety: Leverage TypeScript's type system to the fullest. Avoid bypassing type checks.
  • Readability: Write code for humans first, computers second. Clear naming and structure are more important than clever one-liners.
  • Modern Features: Use modern ECMAScript and TypeScript features (e.g., optional chaining, nullish coalescing) where appropriate.

docs.title: Project Configuration
docs.text:
• Strict Mode: Always enable "strict": true in tsconfig.json. This enables a suite of strict type checking options, including noImplicitAny and strictNullChecks.
  • No Unused Locals/Parameters: Enable "noUnusedLocals": true and "noUnusedParameters": true to catch dead code.
  • Consistent Returns: Enable "noImplicitReturns": true to ensure all code paths in a function return a value.
// Recommended tsconfig.json settings
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,
    "noImplicitAny": true,
    "strictNullChecks": true,
    "noUnusedLocals": true,
    "noUnusedParameters": true,
    "noImplicitReturns": true,
    "esModuleInterop": true,
    "forceConsistentCasingInFileNames": true
  }
}

docs.title: Naming Conventions
docs.text:
• Variables & Functions: Use camelCase.
  • Classes & Interfaces: Use PascalCase.
  • Types & Enums: Use PascalCase.
  • Constants: Use camelCase for local constants, and UPPER_CASE for global, static constants (e.g., configuration values).
  • Booleans: Prefix boolean variables/functions with is, has, should, or can (e.g., isEnabled, hasAccess).
  • Private Members: Do not use the _ prefix for private properties unless specifically required by a framework or to avoid naming collisions with getters/setters. Use the private keyword or # private fields.
  • Filenames: Use kebab-case for all files (e.g., user-profile.ts, api-client.ts). React components may use PascalCase (e.g., UserProfile.tsx).
// Good
const userName = 'Alice';
const MAX_RETRIES = 5;
class UserProfile {}
interface UserData {}
function getUser() {}

// Bad
const User_Name = 'Alice';
const max_retries = 5;
class userProfile {}
interface userData {}

docs.title: Types and Type Safety
docs.text:
• No Any: Avoid any at all costs. It disables type checking. Use unknown if the type is truly not known yet, and narrow it down later.
  • Interface vs Type:
    • Use interface for defining object shapes and public APIs (extensible).
    • Use type for unions, intersections, primitives, and tuples.
  • Explicit Return Types: Always explicitly type function return values, even if they can be inferred. This prevents accidental API changes.
  • No Non-Null Assertion: Avoid the non-null assertion operator (!). Use optional chaining (?.) or proper null checks instead.
  • Readonly: Mark properties as readonly if they shouldn't be mutated. Use ReadonlyArray<T> for arrays that shouldn't be modified.
  • Enums: Prefer union types of string literals over enum for simple sets of values, as they are lighter and closer to JS. Use const enum if performance is critical and values are internal.
// Good
type Status = 'pending' | 'active' | 'inactive';

interface User {
  readonly id: string;
  name: string;
  status: Status;
}

function getStatus(user: User): Status {
  return user.status;
}

// Bad
enum StatusEnum { // Often unnecessary overhead
  Pending,
  Active
}

docs.title: Variables and Constants
docs.text:
• Const vs Let: Use const by default. Only use let if re-assignment is necessary.
  • No Var: Never use var.
  • Destructuring: Use object and array destructuring when accessing multiple properties.
// Good
const { name, age } = user;
const [first, second] = items;

// Bad
const name = user.name;
const age = user.age;

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
• Arrow Functions: Use arrow functions for callbacks and simple functions. Use function declarations for top-level exports or when hoisting is needed.
  • Parameters:
    • Use default parameter syntax (param = defaultValue) instead of mutating logic inside the function.
    • Use a config object (destructured) if a function takes more than 3 arguments.
  • Optional Parameters: Use ? for optional parameters.
// Good
interface SearchConfig {
  query: string;
  limit?: number;
  offset?: number;
}

function search({ query, limit = 10, offset = 0 }: SearchConfig): void {
  // ...
}

docs.title: Control Flow
docs.text:
• Equality: Always use triple equals === and !==.
  • Loops: Prefer map, filter, reduce, find, every, some over for loops. Use for...of if iteration is strictly necessary.
  • Switch: Use switch statements for multiple conditions on the same variable. Ensure all cases are covered (exhaustive check) or a default is provided.
// Exhaustive check example
type Action = { type: 'start' } | { type: 'stop' };

function handleAction(action: Action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'start':
      // ...
      break;
    case 'stop':
      // ...
      break;
    default:
      const _exhaustiveCheck: never = action; // Error if a case is missed
  }
}

docs.title: Data Structures
docs.text:
• Arrays: Use [] shorthand for simple arrays (string[]). Use Array<T> for complex types (Array<string | number>).
  • Maps and Sets: Use Map and Set when keys are not strings or when frequent additions/removals occur.
  • Immutability: Treat data as immutable where possible. Use spread syntax ... to create copies.

docs.title: Classes and OOP
docs.text:
• Access Modifiers: Explicitly use public, private, and protected. Public is default, but being explicit documents intent.
  • Readonly Properties: Mark properties initialized in the constructor that don't change as readonly.
  • Parameter Properties: Use parameter properties in constructors to reduce boilerplate, but maintain readability.
class Person {
  constructor(
    public readonly name: string,
    private age: number
  ) {}

  public getAge(): number {
    return this.age;
  }
}

docs.title: Asynchronous Programming
docs.text:
• Async/Await: Prefer async/await over .then() chains.
  • Promise.all: Use Promise.all to run independent promises in parallel.
  • Error Handling: Use try/catch with await.
  • Top-level await: Use top-level await where supported (modern environments).
// Good
async function fetchData() {
  try {
    const result = await api.get('/data');
    return result;
  } catch (error) {
    console.error(error);
  }
}

docs.title: Modules and Imports
docs.text:
• ES Modules: Always use ES Module syntax (import/export).
  • Import Order:
    1. Built-in Node modules (e.g., fs, path).
    2. External dependencies (e.g., react, lodash).
    3. Internal modules (absolute or relative).
  • Named Exports: Prefer named exports over default exports. This improves refactoring and tree-shaking.
  • Barrels: Use index.ts files (barrel files) sparingly to group exports, but be mindful of circular dependencies.
import path from 'path';
import { useState } from 'react';
import { User } from './models';

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
• Custom Errors: Extend the built-in Error class for custom application errors.
  • Handling Unknowns: When catching errors, remember they are of type unknown. Type guard them or cast safely.
try {
  // ...
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof Error) {
    console.error(error.message);
  }
}

docs.title: Comments and Documentation
docs.text:
• JSDoc: Use JSDoc /** ... */ for public APIs, interfaces, and complex logic.
  • Self-documenting Code: Prefer expressive variable names and clear structure over redundant comments.
  • TODOs: Use // TODO: to mark areas for future work.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• Tools: Use Jest or Vitest for unit testing.
  • File Naming: Test files should be named *.test.ts or *.spec.ts and co-located with the source file or in a __tests__ directory.
  • Descriptive Names: Use descriptive strings in describe and it/test blocks.

docs.title: Recommended Tools
docs.text:
• Linter: ESLint with typescript-eslint.
  • Formatter: Prettier. Configure it to run on save.
  • Compiling: tsc (TypeScript Compiler) or bundlers like Vite, esbuild, or Webpack.
  • VS Code: Use the official TypeScript extension and enable strict null checks in the editor.

docs.title: Related Interview Questions
docs.text: • Practice Questions: Test your knowledge of Typescript concepts.

docs.title: YAML Style Guide
docs.text:
What's on this page

  • Core content for this topic in the Inkorporated enterprise OS.
  • Practical guidance, roles, or standards as applicable.

What this enables

  • Consistent enterprise operations and decision-making.
  • Shared language for humans and cyborg AI agents.

This document outlines the coding standards and best practices for YAML (YAML Ain't Markup Language) files within this project. Adhering to these guidelines ensures consistency, readability, and prevents common pitfalls in configuration files.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
1. General Principles
  2. File Extension and Formatting
  3. Syntax and Structure
  4. Naming Conventions
  5. Data Types
  6. Comments
  7. Keys and Values
  8. Lists and Dictionaries
  9. Multi-line Strings
  10. Anchors and Aliases
  11. Security
  12. Validation and Schemas
  13. Recommended Tools

docs.title: General Principles
docs.text:
• Human Readability: YAML is designed to be human-readable. Prioritize layout and structure that aids human understanding.
  • Consistency: Stick to a single style for quoting, indentation, and key naming throughout a project.
  • Data vs. Code: Remember that YAML is a data serialization language, not a programming language. Avoid complex logic (like excessive anchors/aliases) that mimics code inheritance unless absolutely necessary.
  • DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself): Use anchors and aliases judiciously to reduce repetition, but not at the expense of readability.

docs.title: File Extension and Formatting
docs.text:
• Extension: Use .yaml for all YAML files. Do not use .yml.
  • Indentation:
    • Use 2 spaces per indentation level.
    • Never use tabs.
  • Line Length: Limit lines to 80 characters where possible, or 100 characters max. This matches common editor settings and improves side-by-side diffing.
  • Encoding: Always use UTF-8.
  • End of File: Ensure files end with a single newline character.

docs.title: Syntax and Structure
docs.text:
• Document Separators:
    • Start files with --- (document start marker) if the file might be concatenated or if it helps clarity.
    • Omit --- for simple configuration files where it adds noise.
    • Avoid ... (document end marker) unless strictly necessary for stream processing.
  • Directives: Place directives (like %YAML 1.2) at the very top if used, but they are generally optional for configuration files.

docs.title: Naming Conventions
docs.text:
• Keys:
    • Use snake_case (key_name) as the primary standard for general configuration.
    • Use kebab-case (key-name) if mandated by the specific ecosystem (e.g., Kubernetes, Ansible).
    • Be consistent within a single file and project.
    • Avoid spaces and special characters in keys to prevent the need for quoting.
  • Consistency: Match the naming convention of the application consuming the YAML.

docs.title: Booleans
docs.text:
• Use true and false (all lowercase).
  • Avoid: yes, no, on, off, True, False. The YAML 1.2 spec is stricter, but many parsers still accept 1.1 types. Sticking to true/false is safest and most standard.
# Good
feature_enabled: true
debug_mode: false

# Bad
feature_enabled: yes
debug_mode: OFF

docs.title: Strings
docs.text:
• Unquoted: Use unquoted strings for simple alphanumeric values without special characters.
  • Quoted:
    • Use double quotes " if the string contains special characters, escape sequences (like \n), or starts with a character that could confuse the parser (e.g., [, {, *, #, !, %, @, &, |, >, ?, -, :, ,).
    • Use single quotes ' if the string contains double quotes and no escape sequences are needed.
  • Numbers as Strings: Always quote numbers that should be treated as strings (e.g., versions, account numbers) to prevent them from being parsed as integers or floats.
version: "1.10"  # Good (keeps it a string)
version: 1.10    # Bad (parsed as float 1.1)
country_code: "045" # Good (preserves leading zero)

docs.title: Null
docs.text:
• Use null or omit the value.
  • Avoid ~.

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
• Be explicit.
  • Avoid octal notation (starting with 0) unless intentional and standard-compliant (YAML 1.2 uses 0o).

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
• Style: Use # followed by a space.
  • Placement:
    • Inline: Allowed for short explanations.
    • Block: Preferred for detailed descriptions. Indent block comments to align with the code they describe.
  • Content: Explain why a configuration is set, especially for non-obvious values or workarounds.
# Timeout set to 30s to accommodate slow legacy backend
timeout: 30

retry_count: 5 # Retry 5 times before failing

docs.title: Keys and Values
docs.text:
• Colons: Put a single space after the colon :.
    • Good: key: value
    • Bad: key:value
  • Duplicate Keys: Never use duplicate keys in the same mapping. Most parsers will either error out or silently overwrite the first value.

docs.title: Lists and Dictionaries
docs.text:
• Block Style: Prefer block style (indented) for readability.
# Good
items:
  - item1
  - item2

# Acceptable for short lists
items: [item1, item2]
  • Flow Style: Use flow style ({...}, [...]) only for very short, simple structures that fit on one line.
  • List Items: Indent the hyphen - at the same level as the key or indented by 2 spaces. Pick one style and stick to it.
    • Recommended: Indent list items by 2 spaces relative to the parent key.
# Recommended
users:
  - name: alice
    uid: 1001
  - name: bob
    uid: 1002

# Also common (no indentation for hyphen)
users:
- name: alice
  uid: 1001

docs.title: Multi-line Strings
docs.text:
• Literal Style (|): Preserves newlines. Use for code blocks or embedded scripts.
  • Folded Style (>): Replaces single newlines with spaces. Use for long prose or descriptions.
  • Chomping Indicators:
    • |- or >-: Strip the final newline.
    • |+ or >+: Keep all trailing newlines.
    • Default (no indicator): Keep a single trailing newline.
description: >
  This is a long description that spans multiple
  lines in the YAML file but will be rendered
  as a single line string.

script: |
  echo "Hello World"
  ls -la

docs.title: Anchors and Aliases
docs.text:
• Usage: Use anchors (&name) and aliases (*name) to avoid repetition of large data structures.
  • Merge Keys (<<): Use merge keys to inherit from a base dictionary. Note that merge keys are optional in YAML 1.2, but widely supported.
  • Clarity: Do not overuse. If the hierarchy becomes too deep or complex, it becomes hard to read.
default_settings: &defaults
  timeout: 10
  retries: 3

production:
  <<: *defaults
  timeout: 30

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Safe Loading: When writing code that parses YAML, always use "safe load" functions (e.g., yaml.safe_load() in Python) to prevent code execution vulnerabilities from unsafe tags like !!python/object.
  • Secrets: Do not commit secrets (passwords, API keys) to version control in YAML files. Use templating, environment variables, or secret management tools (e.g., Sealed Secrets, Vault).

docs.title: Validation and Schemas
docs.text:
• JSON Schema: Use JSON Schema to validate YAML configuration files where structure is critical.
  • Linting: Enforce style and syntax checks using CI/CD pipelines.

docs.title: Recommended Tools
docs.text:
• Linter: yamllint
    • Can verify indentation, line length, trailing spaces, and more.
  • Formatter: prettier
    • Supports YAML and enforces consistent formatting.
  • Processor: yq
    • Lightweight and portable command-line YAML processor (like jq for YAML).
  • Validation: kubeval (for Kubernetes), check-jsonschema.

docs.title: Zsh Style Guide
docs.text:
What's on this page

  • Core content for this topic in the Inkorporated enterprise OS.
  • Practical guidance, roles, or standards as applicable.

What this enables

  • Consistent enterprise operations and decision-making.
  • Shared language for humans and cyborg AI agents.

This document outlines the coding standards and best practices for Zsh scripting within this project. While Zsh shares many similarities with Bash, it offers distinct features and default behaviors that require specific attention.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
1. General Principles
  2. File Header and Extension
  3. Formatting and Indentation
  4. Naming Conventions
  5. Variables and Parameters
  6. Arrays and Associative Arrays
  7. Input and Output
  8. Control Flow
  9. Functions and Autoloading
  10. Globbing and Expansion
  11. Error Handling and Robustness
  12. Comments and Documentation
  13. Security
  14. Recommended Tools

docs.title: General Principles
docs.text:
• Leverage Zsh Features: Use Zsh's powerful features (glob qualifiers, recursive globbing, associative arrays) where they improve clarity or performance over standard POSIX sh constructs.
  • Robustness: Scripts should fail early and loudly.
  • Readability: Code should be self-documenting. Use descriptive names.
  • Consistency: Follow the style of the existing codebase.

docs.title: File Header and Extension
docs.text:
• Shebang: Always start with a shebang. 
    #!/usr/bin/env zsh
  • Extension: Executable scripts should generally not have an extension. Library files or sourced scripts should end in .zsh.
  • Mode: Executable scripts must have the executable bit set (chmod +x).

docs.title: Formatting and Indentation
docs.text:
• Indentation: Use 2 spaces for indentation. Do not use tabs.
  • Line Length: Aim for 80 characters, extending to 100 if it improves readability.
  • Pipelines: Break long pipelines across lines, ending with |.
  • Blocks: then, do should be on the same line as the condition/loop command.
# Good
if [[ -f "$file" ]]; then
  print "File exists"
fi

# Good pipeline
ls -1 \
  | grep "pattern" \
  | sort

docs.title: Naming Conventions
docs.text:
• Variables: lower_case for local/loop variables. UPPER_CASE for environment/global variables.
  • Functions: snake_case (e.g., parse_input).
  • Files: kebab-case (e.g., install-deps.zsh).
  • Private Members: Prefix internal functions/variables with _ (e.g., _helper_func).

docs.title: Variables and Parameters
docs.text:
• Declaration: Use local or typeset inside functions to prevent polluting the global scope.
    • Note: In Zsh, typeset is equivalent to local inside functions.
  • Quoting: Unlike Bash, Zsh does not split words on unquoted variable expansion by default. However, always quote strings ("$var") that might contain empty values or if portability habits are desired.
    • Exception: Intentionally unquoted variables for splitting (though explicit splitting flags ${=var} are preferred).
  • Types: Use integer for math variables and float for floating point to enforce typing. 
    integer count=0
local -a items

docs.title: Arrays and Associative Arrays
docs.text:
• Indexing: Zsh arrays are 1-based by default. Do not assume 0-based indexing unless setopt KSH_ARRAYS is widely used (discouraged in pure Zsh scripts).
  • Declaration: 
    # Array
local -a my_list=( "item1" "item2" )

# Associative Array (Map)
local -A my_map
my_map[key]="value"
  • Iteration: 
    for item in "${my_list[@]}"; do
  ...
done

for key value in "${(@kv)my_map}"; do
  print "$key -> $value"
done

docs.title: Input and Output
docs.text:
• Print: Prefer print or printf over echo. print is a Zsh builtin with consistent behavior.
    • print -r prints raw strings (ignores escapes).
    • print -l prints elements separated by newlines.
  • Stderr: 
    print -u2 "Error message"

docs.title: Control Flow
docs.text:
• Conditions: Use [[ ... ]] exclusively. It handles regex (=~) and globbing safely.
  • Arithmetic: Use (( ... )) for math comparisons and operations. 
    if (( count > 5 )); then ... fi
(( count++ ))
  • Loops:
    • for x in ...; do ...; done
    • while ...; do ...; done
    • Short form for loops (e.g., for x (...)) are valid but standard syntax is often more readable for complex blocks.

docs.title: Functions and Autoloading
docs.text:
• Definition: Prefer function_name() { ... }. The function keyword is optional but can be used.
  • Autoloading: For large suites of functions, use autoload -Uz function_name and keep functions in separate files in $fpath. This improves startup time.
  • Return: Return status codes (0-255). Output data via stdout.
my_function() {
  local input="$1"
  if [[ -z "$input" ]]; then
    return 1
  fi
  print "Processing $input"
}

docs.title: Globbing and Expansion
docs.text:
• Recursive Globbing: Use ** freely for recursive searches.
  • Qualifiers: Use glob qualifiers to filter files efficiently without piping to find.
    • *(/): directories only
    • *(.): plain files only
    • *(x): executables
    • *(m-1): modified in the last day 
      # List all regular files recursively
ls **/*(.)
  • Modifiers: Use modifiers like :t (tail/filename), :h (head/dirname), :r (remove extension). 
    local file="/path/to/image.png"
print ${file:t}   # image.png
print ${file:r}   # /path/to/image

docs.title: Error Handling and Robustness
docs.text:
• Options:
    • setopt ERR_EXIT (or set -e): Exit on error.
    • setopt NO_UNSET (or set -u): Error on unset variables.
    • setopt PIPE_FAIL (or set -o pipefail): Check all commands in a pipe.
  • Standard Preamble: 
    emulate -L zsh # Reset options to standard Zsh defaults inside functions/scripts
setopt ERR_EXIT NO_UNSET PIPE_FAIL
  • Traps: Use trap for cleanup. 
    trap 'rm -f $temp_file' EXIT

docs.title: Comments and Documentation
docs.text:
• Header: Scripts should explain their purpose at the top.
  • Functions: Document inputs, outputs, and side effects.
  • Inline: Explain why tricky logic is used.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Eval: Avoid eval.
  • Temporary Files: Use mktemp or Zsh's =(command) substitution if appropriate for temporary file handling.
  • Paths: Use absolute paths for critical commands or ensure $PATH is trusted.

docs.title: Recommended Tools
docs.text:
• Syntax Check: zsh -n script.zsh checks for syntax errors without running.
  • Debugging: zsh -x script.zsh traces execution.

docs.title: Technical Support Knowledge Base
docs.text: Welcome to the Employee Technical Support Knowledge Base. Here you will find guides, troubleshooting steps, and policies related to IT services.

docs.title: Getting Help
docs.text:
If you can't find what you're looking for here, please contact the IT Service Desk:

  • Slack: #help-it (Best for quick questions)
  • Email: support@company.com (For formal tickets)
  • Service Portal: https://support.company.com (To track status)

docs.title: Quick Links
docs.text:
• Password Reset
  • Wi-Fi Access
  • Report Phishing

docs.title: Categories
docs.text:
• Identity & Access: Password resets, MFA, SSO.
  • Connectivity: VPN, Wi-Fi, Network.
  • Hardware: Laptops, Accessories.
  • Software: Licenses, Developer Tools.
  • Collaboration: Slack, Zoom, Email.
  • Security: Phishing, Incident Reporting.

docs.title: Slack Best Practices
docs.text: Slack is our digital HQ. Using it effectively helps reduce noise and increase productivity.

docs.title: Channel Naming Conventions
docs.text:
• #team-NAME: Team-specific discussions (e.g., #team-platform).
  • #proj-NAME: Project-specific (e.g., #proj-migration).
  • #feat-NAME: Feature development.
  • #help-TOPIC: Support channels (e.g., #help-it, #help-hr).
  • #social-TOPIC: Non-work (e.g., #social-pets, #social-gaming).
  • #announce-TOPIC: Read-only announcements.

docs.title: Etiquette
docs.text:
• Threads: Always use threads for replies to keep channels clean.
  • @here / @channel: Use sparingly. Prefer @user or just posting the message.
  • Status: Sync your status with your calendar (Google Calendar app does this automatically).
  • Availability: Respect "Do Not Disturb" hours.

docs.title: Retention Policy
docs.text:
• Public Channels: 90 days.
  • Private Channels: 90 days.
  • Direct Messages: 30 days.

Important: Do not use Slack for long-term documentation or decision records. Use Google Docs or the Wiki.

docs.title: Slack Connect
docs.text: We can connect shared channels with external partners/vendors. Request a Slack Connect channel via #help-it.

docs.title: Video Conferencing (Zoom/Google Meet)
docs.text: We use Zoom as our primary video conferencing tool and Google Meet as a backup.

docs.title: Zoom Setup
docs.text:
1. Login: Use SSO (company.zoom.us).
  2. Plugin: Install the Google Calendar plugin to add Zoom links to meetings automatically.

docs.title: Conference Rooms
docs.text:
• Zoom Rooms: Most meeting rooms are equipped with "Zoom Room" controllers (iPad).
  • Joining:
    1. Book the room in Google Calendar.
    2. Tap "Start" on the iPad controller when you arrive.
  • Wireless Sharing: Use the "Share Screen" button on the controller or enter the "Sharing Key" displayed on the TV.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Camera On: Encouraged for team meetings to build connection.
  • Mute: Mute when not speaking to reduce background noise.
  • Recording:
    • Inform participants before recording.
    • Cloud recordings are retained for 30 days.
    • Sensitive meetings should not be recorded to the cloud.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Audio Issues: Check your input/output device in Zoom settings before the call.
  • Lag: Turn off your camera if your internet connection is unstable.

docs.title: VPN Configuration
docs.text: The Virtual Private Network (VPN) allows you to access internal resources securely when working remotely.

docs.title: VPN Client
docs.text: We use Cisco AnyConnect Secure Mobility Client.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
1. Mac: The client is pre-installed via MDM. Look for the Cisco AnyConnect icon in your Applications folder.
  2. Windows: Pre-installed via Intune.
  3. Linux:
    • sudo apt-get install network-manager-openconnect (or equivalent).
    • Or download the installer from the portal.

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
1. Launch Cisco AnyConnect.
  2. Enter the server address: vpn.company.com.
  3. Click Connect.
  4. Enter your username and password.
  5. Approve the Duo MFA push.

docs.title: Split Tunneling
docs.text: Our VPN uses split tunneling. * Internal Traffic (e.g., Jira, Intranet, internal servers) goes through the VPN. * Internet Traffic (e.g., Google, YouTube) goes directly to the internet. This improves performance.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Connection Failed: Ensure you have a stable internet connection.
  • MFA Timeout: Approve the Duo push promptly.
  • Certificate Error: Re-install the root certificate from the Security Portal.

docs.title: Office Wi-Fi Networks
docs.text: We have two primary Wi-Fi networks in all office locations.

docs.title: Employee Network: Office-Secure
docs.text:
This is the primary network for company-issued devices.

  • SSID: Office-Secure
  • Authentication: WPA2-Enterprise (802.1x) with Certificate.
  • How to Connect:
    • Your laptop should automatically connect via the pushed MDM profile.
    • If prompted, select your user certificate.
  • Access: Full access to internal resources, printers, and the internet.

docs.title: Guest Network: Office-Guest
docs.text:
This network is for personal devices and visitors.

  • SSID: Office-Guest
  • Password: Rotates monthly. Check the digital signage in the lobby or ask the receptionist. Currently: GuestAccess2024!
  • Access: Internet only. No access to internal resources.

docs.title: Troubleshooting Connection Issues
docs.text:
1. "Unable to join network": Forget the network and try re-joining.
  2. Weak Signal: Move closer to an access point (look for the white circular devices on the ceiling).
  3. Certificate Error: If prompted to trust a certificate named radius.company.com, click Trust.

docs.title: Hardware Accessories
docs.text: Employees are entitled to standard peripherals to create a productive workspace.

docs.title: Standard Issue Items
docs.text: You can request these items via the Service Portal without manager approval: * Monitor: 1x 27" 4K Monitor (Dell/LG). * Keyboard: Apple Magic Keyboard or Logitech MX Keys. * Mouse: Apple Magic Mouse or Logitech MX Master 3. * Headset: Jabra Evolve or equivalent. * Adapters: USB-C Hub, HDMI cables.

docs.title: Special Requests
docs.text: Items requiring manager approval: * Additional monitors (up to 2 total). * Vertical mouse / Ergonomic keyboards (Kinesis, ErgoDox). * Standing desk converters. * Privacy screens.

docs.title: How to Request
docs.text:
1. Go to the Service Portal.
  2. Navigate to Service Catalog -> Hardware.
  3. Select the item and add to cart.
  4. Checkout. If approval is needed, your manager will be notified via email.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: If you leave the company or upgrade, accessories over $50 value (monitors, docks) must be returned. Small peripherals (cables, old mice) do not need to be returned.

docs.title: Laptop Refresh Policy
docs.text: We want to ensure every employee has performant hardware to do their best work.

docs.title: Eligibility
docs.text:
• Refresh Cycle: Every 3 years.
  • Early Refresh: Considered for hardware failure or significant role change requiring different specs.

docs.title: Engineering & Design
docs.text:
• Mac: MacBook Pro 16", M3 Max, 64GB RAM, 1TB SSD.
  • PC: Dell XPS 15, i9, 64GB RAM, 1TB SSD, NVIDIA GPU.
  • Linux: Dell Precision (Developer Edition), Ubuntu pre-loaded.

docs.title: Business & G&A
docs.text:
• Mac: MacBook Air 15", M3, 16GB RAM, 512GB SSD.
  • PC: Dell Latitude, i7, 16GB RAM, 512GB SSD.

docs.title: Process
docs.text:
1. IT will notify you 30 days before your eligibility date.
  2. Fill out the Laptop Refresh Form.
  3. Select your preferred OS and shipping address.
  4. Once the new laptop arrives, you have 14 days to migrate your data.
  5. Return the old laptop using the provided shipping label.

docs.title: Data Migration
docs.text:
• Use Box or Google Drive to back up your files.
  • Do not use Time Machine for full system restores across different hardware generations.
  • Run the "Migration Assistant" script provided by IT to move local settings.

docs.title: Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) Setup
docs.text: We use Duo Security for Multi-Factor Authentication to protect company assets.

docs.title: Enrollment
docs.text:
1. Log in to the SSO portal. You will be prompted to enroll in MFA if you haven't already.
  2. Choose "Mobile Device" and enter your phone number.
  3. Download the Duo Mobile app from the App Store or Google Play Store.
  4. Scan the QR code displayed on your screen with the Duo app.

docs.title: Hardware Tokens (YubiKey)
docs.text:
For engineering roles or upon request, YubiKeys are available.

  1. Request a YubiKey via the Accessory Request page.
  2. Once received, insert the key into your USB port.
  3. In the Duo prompt, select "Add a new device" -> "Security Key".
  4. Touch the YubiKey when prompted.

docs.title: Backup Codes
docs.text:
It is highly recommended to generate backup codes in case you lose your phone.

  1. Go to your MFA settings in the SSO portal.
  2. Select "Generate Backup Codes".
  3. Store these in a secure location (e.g., password manager, physical safe). Do not save them on your desktop.

docs.title: Password Reset Procedures
docs.text: Maintaining a secure password is critical. If you have forgotten your password or need to change it, follow the steps below.

docs.title: Self-Service Password Reset
docs.text:
The fastest way to reset your password is via our self-service portal.

  1. Go to https://sso.company.com/forgot-password.
  2. Enter your employee email address.
  3. Complete the MFA verification (SMS or Authenticator App).
  4. Enter and confirm your new password.

docs.title: Manual Password Reset
docs.text:
If you cannot access the self-service portal or are locked out of your MFA device:

  1. Contact the IT Service Desk at support@company.com or call +1-555-0199.
  2. You will need to verify your identity with your manager or via a video call with IT.

docs.title: Password Requirements
docs.text:
• Minimum 12 characters.
  • Must contain uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and special characters.
  • Cannot be one of your last 5 passwords.
  • Must not contain your name or username.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Account Locked: After 5 failed attempts, your account is locked for 15 minutes. Wait or contact IT.
  • MFA Not Working: Ensure your device time is synced.

docs.title: Single Sign-On (SSO) Troubleshooting
docs.text: We use Okta for Single Sign-On to access most internal applications (Slack, Jira, GitHub, etc.).

docs.title: "400 Bad Request" or Loop
docs.text:
• Cause: Corrupted browser cookies or cache.
  • Fix:
    1. Clear your browser cache and cookies for *.company.com and *.okta.com.
    2. Restart your browser.
    3. Try logging in again.

docs.title: "Access Denied"
docs.text:
• Cause: You may not have the required group membership for the application.
  • Fix:
    1. Check if your teammates have access.
    2. Request access via the Software Request process (Access Request in Jira).
    3. Include the specific error message and app name.

docs.title: "MFA Prompt Not Appearing"
docs.text:
• Cause: Ad blockers or browser extensions.
  • Fix:
    1. Disable ad blockers for the SSO page.
    2. Try using Incognito/Private mode.

docs.title: verifying Browser Compatibility
docs.text: Ensure you are using the latest version of Chrome, Firefox, or Safari. Internet Explorer is not supported.

docs.title: Phishing & Security Reporting
docs.text: Security is everyone's responsibility. If you see something suspicious, report it immediately.

docs.title: In Gmail (Preferred)
docs.text:
1. Open the suspicious email.
  2. Click the "Report Phishing" button in the sidebar (or the 3-dot menu > Report phishing).
  3. This automatically quarantines the email and notifies the Security Operations Center (SOC).

docs.title: In Slack
docs.text:
1. Hover over the message.
  2. Click the 3-dot menu.
  3. Select "Report Security Issue".

docs.title: Via Email
docs.text: Forward suspicious emails as an attachment to phishing@company.com.

docs.title: The "Boy Scout Rule"
docs.text: Always leave the code better than you found it.

docs.title: Clean Code Principles
docs.text:
• Meaningful Names: Use intention-revealing names.
  • Functions: Should do one thing, do it well, and do it only.
  • Comments: Do not comment bad code—rewrite it. Comments should explain why, not what.

docs.title: Refactoring
docs.text: Refactoring is the process of restructuring existing computer code—changing the factoring—without changing its external behavior.

docs.title: When to Refactor
docs.text:
• Rule of Three: Three strikes and you refactor.
  • When you add a feature: Refactor to make the feature easier to add.
  • When you fix a bug: Refactor to make the bug obvious.
  • During Code Review: Refactor based on feedback.

docs.title: Technical Debt
docs.text: Technical debt is a metaphor for the accumulation of sub-optimal technical decisions. Like financial debt, it incurs interest (maintenance cost) and must be paid down (refactoring).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Understanding distributed systems is critical for building scalable, reliable applications at our scale.

docs.title: CAP Theorem
docs.text:
• Consistency: Every read receives the most recent write or an error.
  • Availability: Every request receives a (non-error) response, without the guarantee that it contains the most recent write.
  • Partition Tolerance: The system continues to operate despite an arbitrary number of messages being dropped (or delayed) by the network between nodes.

docs.title: PACELC Theorem
docs.text: An extension of CAP that states in case of network partitioning (P) in a distributed computer system, one has to choose between availability (A) and consistency (C) (as per the CAP theorem), but else (E), even when the system is running normally in the absence of partitions, one has to choose between latency (L) and consistency (C).

docs.title: Sharding Strategies
docs.text:
• Key-Based Sharding: Distributing data based on a hash of a key.
  • Range-Based Sharding: Distributing data based on ranges of key values.
  • Directory-Based Sharding: Using a lookup table to find the shard.

docs.title: Consistency Models
docs.text:
• Strong Consistency: Sequential consistency.
  • Eventual Consistency: If no new updates are made to a given data item, eventually all accesses to that item will return the last updated value.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Wheel of Misfortune is a role-playing game used to train engineers on incident response.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
• Practice debugging under pressure.
  • Understand the incident management process.
  • Improve communication during outages.

docs.title: How to Play
docs.text:
1. Game Master: Sets up a scenario based on a past or theoretical incident.
  2. On-Call Engineer: The primary player who must diagnose and resolve the issue.
  3. Scribe: Records the timeline and actions taken.
  4. Communication Lead: Simulates external communication updates.

docs.title: Scenario 1: The Cascading Failure
docs.text: Symptom: Latency spikes on Service A. Root Cause: Retry storm from Service B due to a temporary network blip. Resolution: Implement exponential backoff and circuit breakers.

docs.title: Scenario 2: The Bad Config Push
docs.text: Symptom: Service C is returning 500 errors immediately after a deployment. Root Cause: Invalid YAML configuration file. Resolution: Rollback to the previous version and validate config in CI/CD.

docs.title: Level 1: Public

docs.text: Information for internal use only. * Examples: Employee directory, internal wikis, non-sensitive policies.

docs.title: Level 3: Confidential
docs.text: Sensitive information that requires restricted access. * Examples: Source code, architectural designs, financial reports.

docs.text: Highly sensitive information including Personally Identifiable Information. * Examples: User passwords, SSNs, credit card numbers, health data.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text: We strive for a culture of open, honest, and constructive feedback.

docs.title: The SBI Model
docs.text:
When giving feedback, structure it using Situation, Behavior, Impact: 1. Situation: Describe the specific situation. 2. Behavior: Describe the observed behavior (facts, not assumptions). 3. Impact: Explain the impact that behavior had on you or the team.

Example: "In yesterday's planning meeting (Situation), you interrupted Jane three times while she was presenting (Behavior). This caused her to shut down and we missed her valuable input (Impact)."

docs.title: Radical Candor
docs.text: Care Personally + Challenge Directly. * Obnoxious Aggression: Challenge without Care (brutal honesty). * Ruinous Empathy: Care without Challenge (avoiding conflict to be "nice"). * Manipulative Insincerity: Neither Care nor Challenge (passive-aggressive). * Radical Candor: High Care + High Challenge.

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
This document defines the complete group hierarchy used for User Management and Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). Access permissions in our system are assigned to Groups. Users are members of one or more groups based on their Department, Squad, and Job Role.

The group structure mirrors the Organizational Architecture, ensuring that access rights automatically align with an employee's function and responsibilities.

docs.title: Group Naming Convention
docs.text:
Groups are identified by a unique slug following this convention: group:<type>:<name>

  • Type:
    • org: Top-level organizational units (Departments).
    • team: Sub-departments or functional teams.
    • squad: Cross-functional execution squads.
    • role: Specific job roles (e.g., for role-specific tool access).
    • global: Company-wide groups.
